## F2-169 · An undisclosed substitution written outside `applyMock` — 19 of them, in five shapes

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-169 *(filed 2026-08-09 as [[F2-168]]'s residue; **re-measured before fixing and found 2.4× larger than filed**)* |
| **Module** | `CompliancePage` 9 · `WorkflowsPage` 3 · `FindingDetailPage` 2 · `ControlDetailPage` / `DpiaDetailPage` / `VendorDetailPage` / `EthicsPage` / `PrivacyPage` 1 each · `AdminPage` 1 (reviewed) |
| **Category** | Honesty — fabricated data presented as a server answer, and an error presented as an empty result |
| **Severity** | **P2 High** (filed as P3 on a count of 8; the population and the worst case were both understated) |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09** — one rule, one predicate, four new assertions, mutation 4/4 |
| **⚠ The filing was wrong about its own size** | Filed as *"8 sites in 2 files"* from the F2-168 scan, which only looked for `.catch(() => MAP[realId])`. Measuring the whole class — any fabricated value in a **fallback position**, in any shape — found **20 sites in 9 files**: **15** `.catch(() => MOCK)`, **3** empty-list substitutions, **2** `?? MOCK`. 19 are undisclosed; the 20th is a reviewed exception. 🔑 **A residue noted in passing is a guess about a population, not a measurement of one** |
| **Worst case, which the filing missed entirely** | `frameworkApi.list().catch(() => FRAMEWORKS)` — on *any* failure a signed-in user was shown a **fabricated regulatory catalogue** (8 invented frameworks) with no badge, because this page's `isDemo` is `controls.isDemo \|\| assessments.isDemo \|\| …`, four hook flags that path never touches. `FindingDetailPage` substituted on the **success** path too: `p.content?.find(…) ?? COMPLIANCE_FINDINGS.find(…)` — a real finding list that did not contain the id fell through to a fabricated finding |
| **Three of them are [[F2-166]]'s defect again** | `list.length === 0 ? DISCLOSURES : list` (ethics), `d.length > 0 ? d : WORKFLOW_DEFINITIONS`, `fs.length ? fs : FRAMEWORKS`. A signed-in tenant with genuinely nothing was shown fabricated rows, making the honest empty state **unreachable code**. Measured per tenant in dev: `workflow.definitions` and `ethics.disclosures` hold rows for **organisation 1 only**, so **2 of the 3 dev tenants** (Aramco Trading Company, STC Bank) were being shown 6 fabricated workflow definitions and 6 fabricated conflict-of-interest disclosures apiece. ⚙ The seed script populates one tenant; every empty-list substitution is therefore live for the others — that is the *fifth* instance of this shape and the reason to distrust `length === 0` on sight. (`compliance.frameworks` is **not** tenant-scoped — 24 global rows — so its arm needs a failure, not an empty tenant. Recorded because it is the one of the three that a per-tenant count clears) |
| **The rule** | **Fabricated data may substitute only for a fabricated parent, or when there is no session at all.** [[F2-168]] is what made that expressible: `isDemoId(parentId)` is true exactly when the record the children hang off came out of the corpus. So the six framework tabs, the workflow graph and the four detail pages now gate on `isDemoId`; the page-level demo path stays where it belongs, at the top of the loader as `if (!isAuthenticated()) { … return; }` |
| **The other half of the fix** | Removing a fabrication is not enough: an error rendered as an empty screen is the same lie in a quieter voice. Eight loaders now surface the failure, with a new **bilingual** `loadFailed` string (*"Could not load this list — the request failed. Nothing here is sample data."*) rather than the English literal the 103 existing call sites use |
| **Reviewed exception** | `AdminPage`'s `.catch(() => setRoles(ADMIN_ROLES))` stays, annotated in the guard with the reason: F2-52's comment in that file records that the role *picker* reads `rolesAreReal ? roles : []`, so the ghost roles this fallback contains can never be granted — the Roles tab is a read-only display. If that decoupling goes, the exception goes |
| **Guards** | 4 assertions appended to `demoFallbackContract.test.ts`: a hard zero on ungated fabricated fallbacks (with an anti-vacuity floor of 10 gated survivors, so a scan that stops matching cannot pass), the empty-tenant shape, "a failed load says so" across all 8 loaders, and `loadFailed` present in **both** translation files. Mutation **4/4** |
| **⚠⚠ One of those assertions shipped VACUOUS in its first draft** | `expect(src).not.toMatch(new RegExp(\`length…\\b${n}\\b\`))` — built from a template literal, and it **never matched anything**. Re-inserting the defect left it green; only the general scan caught the mutation. Rewritten with plain substring filters and re-mutated to prove it now fires. 🔑 **A `.not.toMatch` whose regex cannot match is the quietest way to own a guarantee you do not have** — a passing negative assertion looks identical whether the property holds or the pattern is broken. Mutation-test negative assertions *specifically* |
| **⚠ And the instrument mis-classified twice** | Its "does this file have a badge mechanism?" column looked for `applyMock`/`useApiList`, so it reported **False** for `EthicsPage`, which has a hand-rolled `demoMode` — the very flag the substitution bypasses. Then after the fix, 3 of the 13 remaining hits were **comment prose describing the fix**, because the scan did not strip comments: [[F2-165]]'s mistake, repeated with a different scanner |
| **Effort** | M (9 files, 20 sites, 1 new translation key, 4 assertions) |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **A contract that inspects one mechanism certifies only that mechanism.** W2-1b's two guards are correct and were never weakened — they simply had `applyMock` as their whole population, so 19 substitutions written by hand were outside the thing that certified them. The generalisable move is to define the population by **the effect** (fabricated data reaching a render) rather than by **the mechanism** (a particular helper) — the same correction [[F2-165]] made for scans resolving per exported object and [[F2-167]] for a contract about disclosure rather than action |

## F2-170 · Nothing asked whether the endpoint the frontend calls EXISTS — and the answer this time was "all of them"

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-170 *(opened 2026-08-09 out of [[F2-165]]'s dark-method triage, sorted by ENDPOINT as that finding's own correction requires)* |
| **Module** | Platform-wide — 1,782 frontend endpoints against 2,251 controller handlers |
| **Category** | Instrument — a reachability question three existing scans cannot express |
| **Severity** | **P3 Medium** — no defect found; the value is the gate and the corrected figure |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09** — `FrontendEndpointContractTest`, 3 tests, mutation **5/5**, suite 3,468 → **3,471** |
| **The gap** | F2-68(c) asks *"does a screen import this client export?"*, [[F2-165]] asks it per **method**, [[F2-163]] asks *"can the user navigate to this screen?"*. All three look only at the frontend; **none crosses the wire**. So the one thing none of them can see is a client that is imported, called from a live screen, reachable by navigation — and pointed at a path no controller serves |
| **Why it is worth a gate now** | [[F2-158]] is the precedent: `RoleController#list` answered **500 to every caller since it was written** — the whole Role Management API — and nobody noticed because `AdminPage.tsx` wired mock roles into all three failure paths. **The mock fallback was load-bearing.** [[F2-169]] has just deleted 19 of those fallbacks, so a broken path now renders a failure toast instead of plausible rows. The instrument that would have caught F2-158 on day one is this one, and it did not exist |
| **Result — a measured negative** | **0 frontend endpoints have no handler**, across 1,782. Shipped as a **hard zero with no allow-list**, which is only honest while the population is actually zero. The 5 apparent misses were dynamic dispatch over a closed set of literals — `integrationsApi` writes `` `${BASE}/${key}/config` `` where `key` is `'tenable' \| 'crowdstrike' \| 'splunk' \| 'servicenow'` and there is one controller per adapter with the provider in its base path; `workflowRequests` writes `` `/requests/${id}/${action}` `` against literal `/approve`, `/reject`. So a `{}` matches a `{}` **or a literal segment** — a relaxation that removes the need for an allow-list, and an allow-list avoided is worth more than a tighter match ([[F2-61]](c)) |
| **⚠⚠ The scan invented 1,763 defects before it found 0** | First draft, as a regex over controller source: **1,763 of 1,809** frontend endpoints "had no backend handler". Two bugs, each producing a plausible catastrophe. (1) The class-keyword search cut the header **before** the annotations, so no class-level `@RequestMapping` base path was ever read and nothing could match. (2) After fixing that, 160 remained — **48 of them the whole of `/api/v1/cyber`** — because `CyberController`'s javadoc contains *"the former `CyberService` god-class was split"* and `\bclass\s+\w+` matched the prose **"class was"** at offset 1719, before the real annotation at 1934. A live probe answered **200 for every one of the 48**. 🔑 **An extractor that finds nothing looks exactly like a catastrophic defect** — and the only reason I did not file it is that the backend was running and I asked it instead of my own scan |
| **⚠ Prose-as-code, third scanner** | [[F2-165]]'s first draft mis-tokenised a **regex literal**; [[F2-169]]'s scan counted **comment text describing the fix** as violations; this one matched a **javadoc sentence** as a class declaration. The fix is structural, not care: the backend side is now **reflection** over merged annotations off compiled classes, so javadoc is invisible and `@GetMapping` arrives already merged into `@RequestMapping`. Neither of the two bugs above is expressible that way |
| **⚠ And a fourth over-wide pattern, caught by reading the output** | Checking whether these endpoints were role-locked, a bare `'([A-Z_]+)'` over each guard scraped the **module** argument out of `hasPermission('AUDIT','DELETE')` and reported `AUDIT`, `BCM`, `RISK`, `SUST`… as roles absent from `iam.roles` — **21 invented ghost roles and 126 invented "PLATFORM_ADMIN-only" endpoints**. Scoped to `hasAnyRole`/`hasRole` arguments the true answer is **0 and 0**. The module vocabulary and the role vocabulary are different namespaces that look identical |
| **The corrected figure** | **421 backend endpoints have no frontend client** (208 of them **guarded writes**) — the same question F2-165 asks, at endpoint granularity, and **2.2× larger than the 189** that finding publishes: one method can serve several endpoints, and a controller with no client at all has no method to be dark. ⚙ That is F2-165's own lesson turned on F2-165 — *an instrument's granularity is its blind spot, and the blind spot is invisible from inside the instrument.* Also **208 not 163**: a source-regex looking backwards from the mapping never sees a **class-level** `@PreAuthorize`, so 45 governed endpoints read as ungoverned |
| **Ceiling, not a list** | 421 cannot be wired in one slice and an exhaustive red list that size becomes an allow-list nobody reads, so both figures are decrease-only ceilings that also fail when they *drop* — the per-endpoint adjudication stays in F2-165's annotated `KNOWN_DARK`. Not left in prose: an ungateable number stated precisely goes stale ([[F2-162]]) |
| **Guards** | `FrontendEndpointContractTest` (backend suite, hermetic — no DB, no secrets): the hard zero; a matcher control whose **negative case is `POST /risks/{id}/accept`, the bypass [[F2-164]] retired** — a matcher that cannot notice a deliberate retirement cannot notice a typo; and the two ceilings. Anti-vacuity floors on both populations, because a collapsed parser passes a contract trivially. Mutation **5/5**, each caught by the assertion that should have caught it |
| **Triage residue** | The dark-method list was also read for the F2-164/F2-166 shape (a governed step nothing can reach while its successors are wired). **16 entities cannot be created from any screen** — PDPL consents and DPIAs, compliance findings and assessments, ASM assets, crisis-comms templates and audiences, IA plans and engagements, sub-processors, COI campaigns. Measured per tenant in dev, **most exist for organisation 1 only**, so orgs 2–3 can never obtain one. Filed as capability backlog, **not** as an F2-166 repeat: `ConsentRecordService` is the one I read end to end and **nothing else gates on consents**, so no server-side rule goes inert. That distinction is the whole difference between a P2 and a backlog item, and it needs reading the service, not the name |
| **Effort** | M (1 test class, 3 assertions + 3 controls, 5 mutations, 2 baselines) |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **A cross-boundary invariant needs the boundary crossed by the most structural means available.** Everything on the backend side of this contract is available by reflection, and every failure I had came from choosing text. The frontend side has no such option — TypeScript paths are strings — which is exactly why *its* half carries the anti-vacuity floors and the conservative "unresolvable template ⇒ skip" rule |

## F2-176 · Six intake kinds route to a register this platform does not have, and ten HRSD/MOC kinds have no server home at all

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-176 *(filed by [[F2-172]] 2026-08-09, from the one thing that could not be adapted)* |
| **Module** | `lib/intake` catalogue ↔ `module/intake` promotion · DD-88 (HRSD) and DD-94 (MOC) kinds |
| **Category** | Capability gap, now **declared** rather than fabricated |
| **Severity** | **P3** — no data is wrong. The submissions are real, stored and triageable; what cannot happen is promotion, and it now says so |
| **Current State** | ⬜ **OPEN.** Recorded in `IntakePromotionContractTest.TARGETS_WITHOUT_A_REGISTER` with its reason, so the gate fails if the list grows or an entry becomes stale |
| **The measured gap** | Six kinds carry `defaultTarget: 'CONTROL_TEST'` — `CONTROL_ATTESTATION`, `SAUDIZATION_REPORT`, `GOSI_EMPLOYEE_REGISTER`, `WPS_PAYROLL_RUN`, `TASATTUR_SELF_ASSESSMENT`, `CR_ANNUAL_CONFIRMATION` — and **no register exists for one**. Every one is a *periodic regulatory submission*: a Nitaqat headcount return, a GOSI registration, a WPS payroll confirmation, an annual Tasattur self-assessment |
| **⚠ Why `ccm.ControlTestRun` is the wrong home, and this is the whole judgement** | It is the nearest-named thing, and naming is not fit. A `ControlTestRun` is produced by a `ControlTestRunner` — an **automated** continuous-monitoring execution with a registry of runners. Filing a human's monthly Qiwa submission as one would put a manual regulatory filing into an automated-assurance population, which is a fabrication of a different shape: the row would be real and the *classification* false, and every CCM coverage figure would silently include it. Same reasoning that kept [[F2-172]]'s BIA adapter from inventing a critical process |
| **The behaviour change, stated as a regression because it is one** | Before F2-172 these six promoted "successfully" by writing a fabricated row to `localStorage`. They now fail with a **409 naming the target and listing what is supported**. A triager who used to see a green toast now sees an error. That is the correct trade — an error a triager can act on beats a promotion that records a record nobody can find — but it is a visible loss of function and should not be discovered from a support ticket |
| **The wider half** | The ten DD-88/DD-94 kinds have **no server home at all** beyond what F2-172 routed opportunistically: `WORKPLACE_INJURY` and `CONSUMER_COMPLAINT_RESPONSE` to `incident.incidents`, and the three document-shaped ones (`EMPLOYMENT_CONTRACT`, `BENEFICIAL_OWNERSHIP_DISCLOSURE`, `CAPITAL_CHANGE_NOTIFICATION`) to `policy.policy_document`. Nothing in the backend mentions Nitaqat, Qiwa, GOSI, WPS or Tasattur. So the question is not "which table" but whether a **regulatory-filing register** is a product decision worth taking — and that is an owner's call, not an engineering one |
| **Recommendation** | Either build the filing register (a `regreporting`-adjacent table with the submission, the portal it went to, the deadline and the evidence), or re-target these six kinds at something that already exists and accept the classification. Do **not** resolve it by removing the 409 |
## F2-177 · The last three ghost role names were committee seats, and the platform could already tell who held them

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-177 *(opened and closed 2026-08-09 — the fourth and final route out of [[F2-52]], picked because the register said the mechanism did not exist and measuring showed three of its four prerequisites already shipped)* |
| **Module** | `security` (`CommitteeSeatDirectory`, `ModulePermissionEvaluator`) · `module/admin/committee` (`CommitteeSeatAuthority`) · `module/governance` (both controllers) · `module/attachment` (`AttachmentAccessPolicy`) |
| **Category** | Authorisation — an identity-based guard naming an identity nobody can hold, where the identity is a **seat on a body** rather than a job family |
| **Severity** | **P2 High** in the same sense as [[F2-52]]: not a breach, a **capability outage**, and one that is invisible because a guard reciting a role nobody holds is *stricter* than it reads. Here the excluded party is the audit committee, on the views built for it |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09.** Ghost role names in `@PreAuthorize` **3 → 0** (a hard zero, no longer a ratchet); on the attachment surface **3 → 2**, and both survivors are measured extractor artefacts, so **no ghost role name remains on either authorisation surface**. Pure role sites 410 → **404**. Suite +21 tests, mutation **14/14**, live probe **28/28** |
| **What was wrong** | Six read endpoints in `module/governance` recited `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR`, `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER` and `AUDIT_DIRECTOR`. None is a row in `iam.roles`, so each was a permanently false `or` leg. `RiskControlFindingPivotController`'s own javadoc says the view exists for *"engagement scoping and **audit-committee preparation**"* — true of the intent and false of the guard: **the audit committee could not open it.** A seventh site, `AttachmentAccessPolicy`'s `SANCTIONS_CHECK`, carried the same name in a Java role list no `@PreAuthorize` scan sees |
| **Why the previous three routes could not close it** | [[F2-52]] ends with these three because each earlier mechanism is wrong here in a specific way, and the register had recorded that reasoning without acting on it. **Seating** them as roles admits every holder to every committee's business — the same argument D-14 used to refuse `MODEL_OWNER`. **Dropping** the legs is behaviour-preserving and throws away the only surviving record of who the endpoint is for. **Converting** to a module permission hands the same access to everyone with the module read. And **[[F2-159]]'s entity ownership does not fit**: the guarded record is not the committee, it is a pivot or an overview the committee *reviews*, so there is no owner column to consult |
| **The fourth route** | `hasPermission('AUDIT_COMMITTEE','COMMITTEE','SEAT')` — a **second relation** on the four-argument `hasPermission` overload, dispatched on `targetType`, answered by `CommitteeSeatAuthority` against `admin.committee_member_terms`. `targetId` is the committee **type**, not an id, because a guard is written once and every tenant's audit committee has its own primary key |
| **🔑 Three prerequisites had already shipped, for other reasons** | This is the transferable part. [[F2-26]] linked roster seats to platform users; [[F2-28]] made the roster the quorum denominator; **S6c** added `CommitteeSeatOffice` because `committee_member_terms.role` is free text — 16 distinct spellings over 43 seats, three of them meaning *chair*. Not one of those was authorisation work, and together they are everything this needed. ⚙ **The register said "no SpEL function asks the question yet" and treated that as the size of the job; the job was one interface, one component and two queries.** A blocker recorded once decays into a blocker assumed — the cheap move is to re-measure the prerequisites before believing the estimate |
| **⚠ What this does NOT do, and it is the number a reader must see** | Measured 2026-08-09: of **43** seats in dev, **13** name a platform user, **1** is declared external, and **29 do neither**. For `AUDIT_COMMITTEE` the linkage is **0 of 5**. In production it is **0 of 31 — no committee seat is linked to any platform user at all.** So on today's data this predicate answers `false` for every caller, exactly as unreachable as the ghost name it replaces. **The difference is the whole point: a tenant administrator can now fix it from the roster screen instead of needing a jar.** Filed as [[F2-178]] rather than left as a caveat, because a fix whose value depends on data nobody has entered is a fix that needs saying out loud |
| **⚠ The defect this could have rebuilt inside its own remedy** | `hasPermission('AUDIT_COMMITTE','COMMITTEE','SEAT')` — one letter short — fails **exactly** the way a ghost role name fails: no committee of that type, false leg, guard stricter than it reads, nothing complains. **Replacing an unvalidated string with a different unvalidated string is not a fix.** `CommitteeSeatGuardTest` pins the 17-value `committee_type` vocabulary measured in dev at a hard zero, the same way `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest` pins role names, and for the same hermetic reason — the suite has no database |
| **⚠ `AUDIT_DIRECTOR` needed its intent recovered, not its name fixed** | [[F2-52]]'s rule (*"each site needs its intent recovered before its name is touched"*), and it changes the answer. It is not a committee office at all — it is the head of internal audit, whom this platform models as `INTERNAL_AUDITOR`, **already named in the same guard**. So deleting it removed a duplicate rather than an authority, and in dev that person *also* holds a `Standing Invitee` seat on the audit committee, so the seat leg covers them a second way |
| **Three decisions, each stated at the site** | **(a) An observer seat counts.** `Standing Invitee` classifies as `OBSERVER` and is admitted, because on the audit committee that seat is the head of internal audit and the external auditor — the two people most obviously entitled to read an assurance view. Voting membership gates *resolutions*, not reads. **(b) A dissolved committee confers nothing** — dev has `COM-OLD-TECH`, DISSOLVED, with a seat still attached. **(c) The term window is checked**, which is why this does *not* reuse `countActiveSeatsForUser`: that query exists to stop double-seating and deliberately ignores dates, because a future-dated appointment still *occupies* a seat. Authorisation is the opposite question |
| **The third instance of [[F2-156]]'s drift — and the only one that cost nothing** | `AttachmentAccessPolicy`'s `SANCTIONS_CHECK` was still a nine-name role list while `SanctionsScreeningController` has been `hasPermission('AML','READ')` since [[F2-145]](e) slice 5. Measured against `iam.role_permissions`: the **7** roles holding `AML:READ` are *exactly* the 7 real names in the list, so `holders \ registry` was **empty** — nobody could open a sanctions check and 403 on its files, which is what the first two instances caused. The other direction was `{AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER, PLATFORM_ADMIN}`: absent from `iam.roles`, and covered by the bypass. 🔑 **A drift that happens to be harmless is still worth closing, because what made it harmless — two independently maintained lists agreeing — is a coincidence nobody was maintaining.** Reporting it as a third breach would have been false; reporting nothing would have left the coincidence load-bearing |
| **⚠ A stale "measured" corpus, found by re-running the measurement** | `CommitteeSeatOffice.MEASURED_TITLES` was measured 2026-08-03 and pinned at **10** titles. Two days later the CAB/ECAB rosters seeded **six more** and nothing noticed — and its own test could not have: *a title absent from the list is simply not asserted about*, so the corpus growing is invisible from inside the corpus test. All six happen to classify correctly, which is luck; `"CAB Convenor"` would have been `UNCLASSIFIED` and silently missing from a chair-required quorum. Now 16, with both dates, and a test pinning the *consequence* of an unreadable title rather than only the list's size. Same shape as [[F2-172]]'s *"the two catalogues stay in sync"* javadoc |
| **Live probe — 28/28** | `viewer` (VIEWER, named on neither guard) 403 on all six; `auditor` (named on both) not-403 on all six as a control; seat `viewer` on `COM-AUDIT` → **200 on all six**; `term_ends_at` = yesterday with `renewal_status` still ACTIVE → **403**; `term_starts_at` = tomorrow → 403; `ended_at` set → 403; seat on a **DISSOLVED** committee of the same type → 403; seat on an **ACTIVE audit committee in organisation 2** → **403 (cross-tenant isolation proven live, which [[F2-172]] could not do)**; non-voting `Standing Invitee` → 200; and `upsertMapping` with a **valid body** → **403**, so a seat is not authority to redefine the model the committee reviews. 43 seats / 19 committees restored, `CHARINDEX` cleanup |
| **⚠ What the unit suite cannot prove, said rather than implied** | The term-window rule lives in **JPQL**, and the unit suite is database-free by design. `CommitteeSeatAuthorityTest` proves the two halves that layer owns — that the *clock* decides the date asked about ([[F2-160]]), and that every other refusal path is closed — and the window itself is proven only by probe legs 4–6 against real rows. Stated in the test's own header, because [[F2-159]]'s lesson is that a test describing the code accurately can still be describing the wrong thing |
| **Guards** | `CommitteeSeatGuardTest` (3): the six sites must carry the leg, `upsertMapping` must not, no guard anywhere may recite the three retired names, and every seat leg must name a real committee type with the only implemented relation — with an anti-vacuity floor, because a matcher that stops seeing the expression it judges reports a clean surface ([[F2-172]] shipped that failure twice). `CommitteeSeatAuthorityTest` (10). `ModulePermissionEvaluatorTest` +6, including that the two branches never answer for each other and that the administrator bypass short-circuits *before* any roster query. `CommitteeSeatOfficeTest` +1 |
| **⚠ Two anti-vacuity floors had to be lowered, and that is a hazard worth naming** | The role-name floors in `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest` (40) and `RoleNameSurfaceRatchetTest` (18) were calibrated when the populations were larger. This slice legitimately shrank both — 38 names recited, 18 on the attachment surface, i.e. one sitting *exactly* on its floor. A floor that a correct change can breach teaches the next reader to lower it without checking whether the instrument still works, which is how `ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md` drifted nineteen ghosts. Lowered once each, with the measurement recorded beside them: **an anti-vacuity floor is a lower bound on the instrument, not a target for the population** |
| **Effort** | M — 2 new classes, 1 interface, 2 repository queries, 4 guard edits, 21 tests, 14 mutations, 28 probe legs. **No migration**: nothing was catalogued, nothing granted, no schema touched |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **The three names were not three defects — they were one question the expression language could not ask.** Every earlier F2-52 slice adjudicated names one at a time and these three survived six of them, because per-name adjudication cannot produce a new predicate. ⚙ And the mechanism cost about what the second ownership resolver cost ([[F2-161]]), for the same reason: the platform already knew the answer, in a table three other findings had built for other purposes |

## F2-178 · Twenty-nine committee seats name a person with no platform identity and no declaration that they lack one — and in production it is every seat

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-178 *(opened 2026-08-09 by [[F2-177]], which needs this data to be true to be worth anything)* |
| **Module** | `module/admin/committee` (`admin.committee_member_terms.member_user_id` / `no_platform_user`) |
| **Category** | A capability shipped and never adopted — the *data* half of an authorisation feature |
| **Severity** | **P3 Medium**, and rising: it was cosmetic while nothing authorised on a seat. [[F2-177]] now does, and [[F2-145]](c) is queued to |
| **Measured** | Dev: **43** seats — 13 linked to a platform user, **1** declared external (`no_platform_user = 1`), **29 neither**. Per ACTIVE committee: `AUDIT_COMMITTEE` **0/5**, `BOARD` **0/6**, `RISK_COMMITTEE` 2/7, `COMPLIANCE_COMMITTEE` 2/6, `BCM_COMMITTEE` 1/6, `IT_STEERING` 5/9, `EXEC_COMMITTEE` 3/3. Production (`TSS_GRC_Deployment`): **31 seats, 0 linked, 0 declared external** |
| **Why "neither" is the finding** | [[F2-26]] shipped three states on purpose: linked to a user, **declared** to have no platform login (an external director), or unlinked. The third is meant to be transitional. 29 rows in dev and 31 in production have sat in it, so the platform cannot tell *"this director has no login"* from *"nobody has done the linkage"* — and those two have opposite consequences for every rule that consults a seat: the first is a permanent, correct refusal; the second is an outage |
| **What it makes untrue** | [[F2-177]]'s seat guard admits the audit committee **in principle**. On both datasets it admits nobody, so six assurance views remain reachable only by the role names beside the seat leg. Nothing regressed — those role names are untouched — but the intent the leg exists to serve is still unmet in every tenant that exists today |
| **Not fixed here, and the reason is not effort** | Linking a seat asserts *"this named human being is this platform user"*. That is a governance act with an audit trail ([[F2-26]] built the endpoint and the provenance for exactly that reason), not a data-cleanup a remediation slice may perform on a customer's roster. Dev could be seeded; production could not, and seeding only dev would make the instrument look adopted where it is measured |
| **Recommendation** | A **linkage-coverage report** on the committee screen — per committee, seats linked / declared external / neither — plus the same figure in the platform health surface, so the gap is visible to the administrator who can close it. The report is measurable, tenant-scoped and needs no decision; the linking itself stays the tenant's act |
| **⚠⚠ That recommendation was written without measuring, and half of it already existed** | `GET /committees/registry/committees/{id}/linkage` has returned linked / declared-external / unlinked, with a voting split and per-seat detail, **since [[F2-26]]** — and `CommitteeMemberRegistryPage` has rendered a KPI and a warning card from it since the same slice. So the row above described as missing a thing that shipped months ago. 🔑 **This is the same mistake [[F2-177]] recorded as its own headline lesson — *re-measure a recorded blocker before believing its estimate* — made by that slice's own register entry, three hours later.** The lesson does not transfer by being written down: **the register is a claim surface, and a recommendation is the least-verified thing on it.** What was genuinely absent was narrower and is what shipped: the report could only be read **one committee at a time** |
| **What shipped (2026-08-09)** | **(a)** `GET /api/v1/committees/registry/linkage-coverage` (`ADMIN:READ`) — one call, every live committee, with tenant totals. **(b)** `RosterCoveragePanel` on the committees screen, worst-first, self-hiding without `ADMIN:READ`, collapsed to one line when clean, each row linking to the screen that fixes it. **(c)** A **third state**: `hasRoster = false`. **(d)** The two-numbers disclosure below. No migration, no schema change |
| **🔑 The state a per-committee report structurally cannot show** | `linkage(committeeId)` takes an id, so "this committee has an empty roster" and "this committee is 0% linked" arrive as the same screen. They are different defects: an empty roster **can never be quorate**, no resolution it records would be valid, and `ChangeGovernanceHealthService.ROSTER_EMPTY` already refuses CAB approvals for it. Measured 2026-08-09: **9 of 18** live dev committees and **11 of 17** production committees have no term rows whatsoever. A report keyed by committee id cannot count them, and looping it cannot either — the absence is only visible from the committee list side |
| **⚠⚠ The second defect this slice found, and it is the one with a date on it** | F2-26's report counts a seat by `renewal_status = 'ACTIVE'` alone. [[F2-177]]'s seat guard *also* requires `ended_at IS NULL` and that today fall inside the term window. **Two consumers of one column, deciding "this seat counts" by different rules, with nothing reconciling them** — so a roster can read **100% covered and admit nobody**. The tree already carried the rule this breaks, written for a different pair: `ChangeGovernanceHealthService` says *"a report describing access must share its predicate with the enforcement point"*, after [[F2-62]] cost exactly that drift. ⚠ The divergence is **0 rows today** in dev and production, and that is not reassurance: **nothing in this platform ever transitions an ACTIVE term to EXPIRED** — `CommitteeScheduledSweep` only fires 90/60/30-day reminders and `endTerm` is a manual act — so once a window closes the row reads ACTIVE for ever. **The earliest production term ends 2027-03-01.** It arrives by calendar arithmetic, with no code change and nobody's mistake |
| **How the two rules were made one** | `CommitteeMemberTermRepository.CURRENT_SEAT_WINDOW` is a compile-time constant, and both the guard's query and the coverage aggregate are **built from it by concatenation** — one text, not two copies pinned by a test. `SeatLinkageReport` gained `currentSeats`/`currentLinked` beside `linked`, and `Seat.currentlySeated` per row; the registry screen fires a card only when the two disagree. ⚠ `currentlySeated` is a **flag beside `state`, not a fourth `State` value**: currency and linkage are independent axes, and a `LAPSED` enum member would force a lapsed-*and*-unlinked seat to report only one of its two problems |
| **⚠ A trap the shared constant introduced, worth 30 seconds of anyone's time** | Java strips incidental **trailing** whitespace from each line of a text block, so `SUM(CASE WHEN """ + CURRENT_SEAT_WINDOW` emitted `WHENt.endedAt` — and a malformed `@Query` fails at **context startup**, taking the whole application down rather than one endpoint. Both constants now **begin with their own newline**, so no caller can lose the separator, and `SeatWindowPredicateSharingTest` pins that. Measured: it is exactly how the first draft failed |
| **Guards** | `SeatWindowPredicateSharingTest` (9) — the window is exactly its three conditions and mentions no `renewal_status`; both consumers are built from the constant; **every `@Query` binding `:on` must use it**; and *the clause may appear in the repository source exactly once*, so a future author who copies it instead of referencing it fails the build. `CommitteeRosterCoverageTest` (13) — the no-roster state, the fully-lapsed 100%-and-admits-nobody case, external seats leaving the denominator, DISSOLVED excluded *and counted*, worst-first ordering, `SUM`-over-empty-group NULLs coalesced, and the tenant+clock the aggregate is called with. `rosterCoverageSurface.test.ts` (10) |
| **⚠ What the unit suite still cannot prove** | The window lives in JPQL and the suite is database-free, so the textual assertions prove *the same string reaches both queries*, not that JPQL and `CommitteeMemberTerm#isCurrentOn` agree semantically. That is proven by probe leg 8 (every committee's `currentLinked` against the guard's own SQL) and leg 17 (the Java path against the SQL path on a deliberately lapsed seat). Said in the test header, because [[F2-159]]'s decoy survived by describing the code accurately |
| **Live probe — 30/30** | `viewer` 403, unauthenticated 401, `admin` 200; every row's `seats`/`linked`/`currentLinked` matched independent SQL; DISSOLVED excluded and counted; 9 no-roster committees named; `AUDIT_COMMITTEE` reported as admitting nobody. Then the divergence **forced on real data**: a linked term's `term_ends_at` set to yesterday with `renewal_status` untouched → roster count **2 → 2**, coverage **29% → 29%**, guard count **2 → 1**, that seat flagged `currentlySeated: false` while still `LINKED`, and no other seat affected; `ended_at` set → same drop, roster count still unmoved. Cross-tenant: a second-tenant `AUDIT_COMMITTEE` **created for the probe**, one of its seats linked to an organisation-1 user id → absent from the report, every total unchanged, and this tenant's `AUDIT_COMMITTEE` count unmoved |
| **⚠ A cleanup bug the probe's own instrument caught** | The org-2 fixture tagged `[REVIEW-TEST]` in `name_en` and the `DELETE` matched on `code` (`COM-AUDIT-T2-REVIEWTEST` — no bracket literal), so a committee and two seats were **orphaned in another tenant**, and the tag-check leg passed while it happened. What caught it was printing the before/after org-2 count. 🔑 **The `[REVIEW-TEST]` + `CHARINDEX` convention only holds if the tag is in the column the cleanup matches on** — the pattern was right and the column was wrong. The leak is now a **failing leg**, not a printed line |
| **Status** | 🔶 **THE GAP IS NOW VISIBLE; THE DATA IS STILL MISSING.** Production remains **0 of 31 seats linked** and **11 of 17 committees with no roster** — linking a seat asserts *"this named human being is this platform user"*, a governance act with an audit trail ([[F2-26]] built the endpoint and the provenance for exactly that), not a data-cleanup a remediation slice may perform on a customer's roster. What changed is that an administrator can now see it in one place instead of seventeen. **Remaining, and it is an owner/tenant act, not an engineering one:** somebody has to do the linking |
| **⚠⚠ CORRECTION 2026-08-10 — two of this slice's own tests were wrong for three hours of every day, and the suite said so a day after they merged green** | `CommitteeSeatLinkageTest` built its seat-currency fixtures with `LocalDate.now()`, which resolves in the JVM's default zone (Riyadh, **UTC+3**), while `CommitteeMemberRegistryService` reads `LocalDate.now(clock)` with `Clock.system(ZoneId.of("UTC"))`. Between local midnight and 03:00 those differ by a day, so a term ending "yesterday" was still current to the service and `currentSeats()` returned **2 where 1 was asserted**. Surfaced during [[F2-175]]'s full-suite run at **00:4x local**, inside the three-hour window — the only reason it was ever seen. Fixed by injecting `Clock.fixed` on a pinned `TODAY` (2027-06-15), which is what `CommitteeRosterCoverageTest` did from the start. 🔑 **This is the same lesson F2-178 already recorded, from the other side.** That row says *a fixed-clock test whose fixed date equals the real date proves nothing about clock injection*; this says **a test that reads the wall clock at all is asserting against a "now" the code does not share.** One remedy covers both: inject the clock and pin the date. ✔ **Checked and clean in production code:** `CommitteeSeatAuthority` (the guard) and `CommitteeMemberRegistryService` (the report) both use `Clock.system(ZoneId.of("UTC"))`, so they share the zone as well as the predicate — the F2-62 divergence this finding closed has **not** reopened through the clock. ⚙ And the reason mutation did not catch it: the harness ran six named test classes, and this was not one of them — **a mutation harness scoped to the slice's own tests cannot see a slice's own test being wrong about the world.** |

## F2-173 · Two intake kinds share a reference-code prefix, so a submitter cannot tell their tracking codes apart

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-173 *(opened 2026-08-09 by [[F2-172]]'s catalogue parity work — found by asserting a property nobody had asserted, not by a bug report)* |
| **Module** | `module/intake` (`IntakeKindRouting`) + `lib/intake.ts` (`INTAKE_CATALOG`) |
| **Category** | Ambiguous user-facing identifier |
| **Severity** | **P4 Low** — cosmetic today, and bounded: `reference_code` uniqueness is enforced by the column, so nothing collides in the database |
| **What is wrong** | `codePrefix` is documented as *"Two-letter code prefix **per intake kind** for human-friendly tracking codes"*, and `CHANGE_REQUEST` and `CR_ANNUAL_CONFIRMATION` both use **`CR`**. So a submitter holding `CR-XXXX-YYYY` cannot tell an ITIL change request from an MOC commercial-registry annual confirmation, and neither can a support agent reading it aloud. Both codebases agree on the value, so this is **not** a parity defect: the collision is in the design, and F2-172's parity test correctly reports the two catalogues as consistent. |
| **How it is contained** | `IntakeCatalogueParityTest.referenceCodePrefixesCollideExactlyOnce` ceilings the population at **1** and names the pair, so a second collision fails the build. That is deliberately a ceiling rather than a fix: changing a documented reference-code prefix is a user-visible decision, and it does not belong in a parity slice. |
| **Status** | ⬜ **OPEN — needs a product call.** `intake.intake_records` held **0 rows** in dev on 2026-08-09, so no issued code would be invalidated by renaming one of the two today; that window closes the moment the substrate is used. `CC` is taken (`CAPITAL_CHANGE_NOTIFICATION`); `AC` and `RC` are both free. |

## F2-174 · Every intake is routed to a stakeholder code that resolves to nobody

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-174 *(opened 2026-08-09 out of [[F2-172]] — noticed while reading the routing table the parity test now pins)* |
| **Module** | `module/intake` (`IntakeKindRouting.defaultAssignee` → `intake_records.assigned_to`) |
| **Category** | A control declared, then enforced at no writer — **RC-F**, and the same shape as [[F2-94]]'s recipient keys one table over |
| **Severity** | ~~**P3 Medium**~~ → **P3 Medium, and latent rather than live** — the field is the only record of who owes the SLA decision and it named nothing, but **0 intake records existed in either database**, so nothing had yet been misrouted (see the corrected row below) |
| **What is wrong** | `assigned_to` is set on every submission from a fixed per-kind string: `DPO`, `CSIRT`, `RISK_OFFICER`, `TPRM_LEAD`, `ETHICS_CTE`, `CAB`, `HR_LEAD`, `COMPLIANCE_LEAD`, `POLICY_OFFICER`, `BCM_LEAD`, `AUDIT_LEAD`, `CISO_OFFICE`, `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`. These are **stakeholder codes, not roles**: `TPRM_LEAD` is one of F2-52's ghosts ([[F2-156]] found it live after leaving every guard), `CSIRT` and `ETHICS_CTE` and `CISO_OFFICE` and `CAB` are team labels that exist in no `iam.roles` row, and **nothing in the platform routes, notifies or authorises on the column.** So the inbox displays an owner for a statutory clock and no person is addressed by it. |
| **⚠ "Why it matters now rather than before" was the one false sentence in this row** | It read: *"It is now written on every submission, including the ones carrying a 24-hour GOSI deadline and a 72-hour PDPL breach window."* Measured 2026-08-11 before writing any code: **`intake.intake_records` held 0 rows in dev and 0 in prod.** Nothing had ever been submitted through the rewired substrate, so the field had never been written once — the defect was **latent, not live**. That is the identical error [[F2-175]]'s filing made in the other direction (calling a bypass *"currently benign"* when the supportable claim was *"unexercised"*), and it is worth naming twice because it changes what the fix is allowed to cost: with 0 rows there is **no data migration and no back-fill**, and the whole finding is a rename. 🔑 **"It is written on every submission" and "a row exists" are different claims, and only the second one is a measurement.** |
| **The comparison that makes the shape familiar** | [[F2-94]]: 127 of 140 escalation rule codes reached nobody, and the fix was a **closed vocabulary plus a ratchet over every migration**, not one more key. The same two options were offered here: resolve each code to a role or a committee and fail closed when it does not resolve, or drop the column and route through the workflow engine that F2-94 taught to reach people. |
| **⚠⚠ Both filed options were non-viable as written, and measurement is what showed it** | **(a) "resolve to a role or a committee and fail closed"** — at filing time 10 of 14 codes resolved to nothing, carrying **22 of the 26 kinds**, so failing closed at runtime would have refused a security-event report, a privacy breach and the 24-hour GOSI injury notification over a **routing label**. That directly contradicts the ADR-010 exception F2-172 had just argued for on the same endpoint: *filing is a duty, reading is a privilege.* And the *"or a committee"* half had nothing behind it — **0 of 14 codes match any `admin.committees` row by type, code or name**, in either database, so the [[F2-177]] seat machinery could not have been reused here. **(b) "drop the column and route through the workflow engine"** — `workflow.recipient_list_members` is **empty in dev and in prod**, so that destination has no data behind it either; it would have replaced a label that resolves to nobody with a lookup that returns nobody. 🔑 **A filed row's two "candidate fixes" are the least-verified thing in it after its recommendations — nothing has executed either one.** |
| **✅ What shipped (worked 2026-08-11)** | The third option measurement produced, which neither filed option mentions: **all 14 codes already had a real counterpart seated in `iam.roles`**, so the fix is a rename, not a design. ① 11 assignee slots rewritten in **both** catalogues — `CISO_OFFICE`→`CISO`, `ETHICS_CTE`→`ETHICS_OFFICER`, `CSIRT`→`IR_LEAD`, `RISK_OFFICER`→`RISK_MANAGER`, `COMPLIANCE_LEAD`/`POLICY_OFFICER`→`COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`, `TPRM_LEAD`→`SUPPLIER_MANAGER`, `BCM_LEAD`→`BCM_MANAGER`, `AUDIT_LEAD`→`INTERNAL_AUDITOR`, `CAB`→`CHANGE_MANAGER`; `DPO`/`HR_LEAD`/`ETHICS_OFFICER`/`COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` already correct. 14 distinct codes → **11 real role names**. ② `IntakeAssigneeRoleResolutionTest` — a **hard zero**, reading the one pinned role catalogue. ③ Mutation **11/11**, 0 undeclared survivors. ④ Live probe **55/55** across 11 kinds: submitted, `assignedTo` in the response, `assigned_to` as stored, a real `JOIN` to `iam.roles`, and the TRIAGING history note. |
| **② Where the "fail closed" half actually belongs** | Not at runtime, at **build time**. A hard zero over a 14-value catalogue that ships in a jar means the situation cannot arise in production at all, which is strictly stronger than refusing a submission when it does — and it does not put a statutory intake behind a label lookup. The gate reads `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest.ROLE_CATALOGUE`, the single pinned copy that [[F2-156]]'s surface #2 test already reads, making this its **third reader and not a third copy**; the class's own comment gives the reason (*"a duplicated catalogue is how the census document drifted nineteen ghosts behind the build"*). A second, deliberately weaker assertion checks each of the 11 names appears somewhere in the migration corpus — because the commit that adds an intake assignee is exactly the commit that would add the same fictional name to the pinned copy, and **two edits by one author in one commit are not two sources.** |
| **⚠⚠ A test asserted the defect as correct, and its comment argued for it** | `IntakeSystemSubmissionTest.assigneeIsTheCataloguedStakeholder` pinned `assertThat(saved().getAssignedTo()).isEqualTo("RISK_OFFICER")` under the comment *"assigned_to holds stakeholder codes; a role name in it routes to nobody, and there was never any reason for the two vocabularies to agree."* Every clause of that is backwards: measured, it is the **stakeholder code** that routes to nobody, and a role name is the only value a tenant administrator can attach people to. A second site in the same class pinned the same string inside the history note. **Third instance of the same shape** after [[F2-159]]'s decoy and F2-175's own `startsWith("ISS-")`: 🔑 *a test written by reading the implementation can only agree with it* — and this one was written by me, in the slice that filed this finding. |
| **⚙ The closure with F2-175, worth stating because it inverts that slice's own caveat** | F2-175 deleted a hard-coded `RISK_MANAGER` and replaced it with the catalogue's `RISK_OFFICER`, and its row honestly recorded that this made resolvability **worse** (*"do not read it as 'the assignee now works'"*). With the catalogue now saying `RISK_MANAGER`, both facts are true at once. 🔑 **The hard-code F2-175 removed was right about the name and wrong about the mechanism**; a value can be correct and still worth deleting for where it lives, and the fix for that is to make the single source correct — not to keep the copy. |
| **⚠ Prod does not hold one of the eleven, and that is deployment lag rather than a defect** | `ETHICS_OFFICER` (used by `SPEAKUP` and `ETHICS_DISCLOSURE`) is seated by **V362**, and the deployed server is at Flyway head **V344** with V345–V375 pending (**O-1**) — 58 active roles there against 69 in dev. So on prod today that one name resolves only after the next jar carries its migrations. Recorded rather than worked around: routing ethics disclosures to `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` instead would have made the number look clean on an un-migrated database by **changing who triages a whistleblowing report**. ⚙ Measuring prod at all is [[F2-183]]'s rule (*"measure PROD, not just dev, before shipping"*) applied to a Java constant instead of an `ADD CONSTRAINT` — and it is the only reason this was known before shipping. |
| **⚠ The honest limits, stated because the alternative is a row that reads as more than it is** | ① **Naming a real role is not reaching a person.** Of the 11, exactly **4** have an active holder in dev (`CISO`, `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`, `INTERNAL_AUDITOR`, `RISK_MANAGER`) and the same 4 in prod. That is [[F2-178]]'s caveat exactly — *the mechanism works and the data does not exist yet* — with the difference that it is now a roster question a tenant administrator can answer from the Roles screen, which a name absent from the catalogue never could be. ② **Nothing resolves the column yet:** `assigned_to` reaches `IntakeRecordDto` and renders as a label in the acknowledgement text and the audit note; no queue, notification or guard consults it. ③ A concrete obstacle for whoever wires that: **the two columns collate differently** — `intake.intake_records.assigned_to` is `Latin1_General_100_CI_AS_SC_UTF8`, `iam.roles.role_name` is `SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS`, so a bare join raises *"Cannot resolve the collation conflict … in the equal to operation"* (468/8180) and any resolver must `COLLATE` explicitly. Found by the probe, not by reading. ④ A **per-tenant** stakeholder→role/committee mapping (so one customer's `IR_LEAD` can be another's SOC committee) remains an owner decision and is not what this slice built. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-11.** 14 codes → 11 real role names in both catalogues, hard-zero gate, mutation 11/11, live probe 55/55, suite **3,731/0/0**, FE typecheck clean + 487/487. The defect as filed — *a code that resolves to nobody* — is gone in every deployment that has run V362. Delivery (a queue or a notification that consults the column) was never part of this finding and is not claimed. |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **When a filing offers two designs, measure the population before choosing — the answer may be that neither is needed.** Both options here were architecturally reasonable and both were wrong: one would have refused statutory submissions, the other pointed at an empty table, and the actual fix was a rename that neither considered because nobody had checked whether the real role names already existed. ⚙ And the counterweight, so this is not read as "always just rename": the reason a rename suffices is that **`assigned_to` is a label today**. If it ever authorises or delivers, the [[F2-177]] question returns — *is this a job family or a body?* — and for `CSIRT` and `CAB` the honest answer was a body, which is why they were team labels in the first place. |

## F2-180 · Twelve of the thirteen promotion adapters have never run against a real database — and the first one tried was broken

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-180 *(filed 2026-08-10 — the generalisation of the `CK_risks_status` failure [[F2-175]]'s live probe hit)* |
| **Module** | the 13 `RegisterPromotionPort` adapters across 11 modules (`risk/intake`, `privacy/intake`, `bcm/intake`, `tprm/intake`, `ethics/intake`, `incident/intake`, `policy/intake`, `compliance/intake`, `audit_eng/intake`, `change_adapters`) |
| **Category** | Coverage claimed by reasoning where only execution can establish it — the [[F2-158]] shape (a handler that had answered 500 since it was written) applied to a fan-out |
| **Severity** | **P2 High on the evidence available** — 1 of 1 sampled adapters was broken, and each one is the *only* route by which its register receives a promoted submission |
| **What is wrong** | [[F2-172]] built promotion as 13 adapters, each constructing a register record through its module's own service. Its verification live-probed **one** — `DpiaPromotionAdapter` — end to end, and reasoned about the other twelve from their source, which is a defensible thing to do and is not the same as knowing. F2-175's probe then exercised a second one, `RiskPromotionAdapter`, and it **failed on a CHECK constraint**: it passed `status = "IDENTIFIED"`, which `CK_risks_status` has never allowed. So promoting a `RISK_ISSUE` had never once succeeded. The remaining **eleven** are in exactly the state `RiskPromotionAdapter` was in an hour before it was measured. |
| **Why source review cannot settle it** | Every one of these adapters hands a **string** to a service, which maps it to a column carrying a `CHECK` the Java side never mentions. There is no compiler error, no failing unit test (the services are mocked), and `IntakePromotionContractTest` checks the *wiring* — that a target has a port, that the port returns an id it wrote, that permissions are declared — not that the values the port supplies are ones the schema accepts. A first attempt at a static sweep here compared each adapter's uppercase literals against **every** CHECK in the database and reported `RiskPromotionAdapter` as clean, because `IDENTIFIED` is a legal value of some *other* table. ⚠ **A cross-check that is not scoped to the target table is worse than none — it answers "clean" for the one case known to be broken.** |
| **The two candidate fixes, and the tradeoff** | **(a) Live-probe all thirteen** — one valid submission per kind, promoted, with the created row read back. Decisive, and it is the only thing that would have caught this; costs an integration-test harness under `-Pit` (which already exists for the committee golden path, W1-5). **(b) A schema-aware static pin** — for each adapter, resolve the target entity's table and assert every vocabulary literal it supplies is in that table's CHECK, read from the migrations so the unit suite stays hermetic. Cheaper to run, but it must resolve adapter → service → entity → `@Table` correctly or it will report false confidence, which is the failure mode above. **(b) plus a golden-path IT for the two or three highest-value registers** is probably the honest answer. |
| **Not in scope for F2-175, and why that is not a dodge** | F2-175 fixed the adapter its own chain traverses, because leaving it broken would make that slice's central claim — *the drift issue can now be escalated into the risk register* — false. Fixing eleven more means eleven judgement calls about what each register's "raised, not yet assessed" state is called, each of which is a governance question in the shape of a string literal (`IDENTIFIED` was wrong about the vocabulary and **right about the intent**). That is a slice, not a footnote. |
| **✅ What shipped (worked 2026-08-11)** | **Both (a) and (b).** ① The scoped measurement: 13 adapters → 13 target tables → **18 single-column CHECK vocabularies**, each literal compared against **its own** table's constraint. ② Two more broken adapters found and fixed. ③ `PromotionVocabularyTest` — a hermetic pin reading the migrations, with a registry that refuses an unlisted adapter. ④ The live probe: **50/50 legs, 13 of 13 adapters** submitting → promoting → reading the created row back by the id the server stamped. ⑤ The error-547 diagnostic that had misreported all of this. |
| **② The two it found** | **`VendorPromotionAdapter` wrote `status = "ONBOARDING"`, which `CK_vendors_status` has never allowed** (`ACTIVE\|INACTIVE\|PENDING_REVIEW\|TERMINATED`) — so promoting a `VENDOR_ONBOARDING` submission had **never once worked**, and all 28 vendors in dev are `ACTIVE`, which is what a register looks like when nothing has entered it through the front door. Fixed to `PENDING_REVIEW`, the member of the vocabulary that means what the javadoc argued for. ⚠ **This is the third adapter with one shape**: `IDENTIFIED`, `ONBOARDING`, and the incident category below were each chosen for what they *mean*. Every meaning was right. 🔑 **Being right about what a state means is not evidence about what the column stores it in.** |
| **② and the worse one** | **`IncidentPromotionAdapter` passed the submitter's own category through untouched**, and `CK_incidents_category` accepts five values. Measured against the forms those four kinds render: `SECURITY_INCIDENT` offers `PHISHING\|MALWARE\|LOST_DEVICE\|UNAUTHORISED_ACCESS` — **0 of 4 legal**, so the flagship NCA ECC 6.1 employee-reporting path failed for every submission that answered the question; `WORKPLACE_INJURY` supplies `injuryType` (0 legal) with the constant fallback `"HSE"` (not legal); `CONSUMER_COMPLAINT_RESPONSE` supplies `complaintCategory` (**1 of 5** legal) with fallback `"CONSUMER"` (not legal); `VRP_DISCLOSURE` has no category field, fell through to `CYBER`, and was **the only one of the four that could ever promote**. Fixed by mapping the four form vocabularies onto the column's, per-kind fallbacks, and keeping the reporter's own word on the record — the V261 precedent, whose comment is the clearest statement of the rule in the tree: *"category → 'CYBER' (CK_incidents_category is strict; type kept in description)"*. |
| **🔑 Why severity was never broken, and that is the finding** | Five constrained columns are fed by one accessor, `IntakePromotionContext#severityOrMedium()`, which **clamps** to the four bands every one of them declares. It was written by somebody who had checked. Category, status and change-type had no such accessor. **F2-180 found three broken adapters and not eight because of one clamp** — so the fix is not "be careful with literals", it is **a closed column needs a closed writer, and the clamp is the only place that can be.** `ck_change_type` was clamped in this slice too although it was never failing: the form happens to offer exactly the legal three, which is a fact about today's frontend and not a property of the server. |
| **⑤ The diagnostic that hid all of it** | **SQL Server error 547 is BOTH `FOREIGN KEY` and `CHECK`**, and `GlobalExceptionHandler` answered with the foreign-key wording for both — *"either something it refers to does not exist, or the record is still referenced elsewhere"*. Its own comment read `// FOREIGN KEY / CHECK constraint`, so the ambiguity was known and one of the two was written for. Cost, measured: F2-175 spent a probe iteration being told a promotion had failed on a **reference** in `risk.risks`, a table with **no foreign keys at all**; F2-180 hit the same sentence on `CK_vendors_status`; and then **19 more times** while measuring [[F2-181]]. Three investigations from one wrong noun. Now `conflictKind: VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED` and *"One of the values supplied is not one this field accepts … (column 'category')"* — the column is the one thing the caller cannot infer, and the 547 CHECK message carries it **without** the offending value, so naming it stays inside SEC-CFG-001. 🔑 **A diagnostic that is wrong in a specific, plausible direction is worse than a vague one: it does not slow the reader down, it sends them somewhere.** |
| **What the pin does that a ratchet could not** | Each adapter declares its target table, and each constrained column is **either** bound to the constant holding the value **or** listed in `unwritten` with a reason. That makes the six targets whose tables carry **no** CHECK today (`DPIA`, `BREACH`, `DSR`, `BIA`, `ETHICS_CASE`, `ENGAGEMENT`) into a pin rather than an omission: add a CHECK to `privacy.dpia` and the build fails until somebody has looked at `DpiaPromotionAdapter`. Mutation-tested **15/15**, including the two legs that matter — binding `RiskPromotionAdapter` to *another table's* `CK_incidents_status` (whose vocabulary **does** contain `OPEN`, so only the table-scoping leg can catch it) and adding a CHECK to a target that has none today. |
| **⚠⚠ The unscoped-sweep mistake happened twice more, in one session** | Once as recorded above, and then **again inside this slice**: a heuristic pairing UI option-lists to columns by value overlap produced 30+ "findings", including `VALID_NDI_TABS` (a list of NDI tab names) paired with `ck_change_risk` because both contain `CRITICAL\|HIGH\|MEDIUM\|LOW`. Discarded rather than reported; only the two **same-register** pairings survived into [[F2-181]], each proven with a live POST. And a third time in the pin's own parser, which extracted a column named **`PEND`** from `ratification_state <> N'PENDING'` — because `PENDING` contains `IN`, and `IN` was one of the operators it matched. The `noUndeclaredConstrainedColumn` leg failed on its **first run** and named the phantom column. 🔑 **A regex over SQL that has not had its string literals removed is parsing two languages at once** — and the anti-vacuity habit has now paid for itself twice, after F2-175's `.replace("N","")` turned `OPEN` into `OPE`. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-11.** **13 of 13 adapters verified live** (was 1 of 13), 3 found broken across F2-175+F2-180 and fixed, 18 constrained columns pinned hermetically, mutation 15/15, suite 3,602/0/0. The one probe leg that read as a failure was **the probe's own** assumption — `ENGAGEMENT` returns the `external_id`, not a bigint, exactly as `RegisterPromotionPort`'s javadoc allows — and was corrected rather than explained away, because *a false negative in a verification artefact is worse than no leg, since it gets quoted*. |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **"I read the code and it looks right" is a claim about the code; "I ran it" is a claim about the system.** F2-172 was unusually careful — it measured the guard population, the catalogue divergence and the permission matrix before writing anything — and still shipped a broken adapter, because the one thing it did not do for twelve of thirteen paths was execute them. ⚙ And the corollary for fan-out work: **verifying one branch of a fan-out establishes the mechanism, not the branches.** The mechanism was fine — all three defects were in the values, and the mechanism carried them faithfully to a database that refused them. |

## F2-181 · The incident register's own screen offers 22 categories and the column accepts 3

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-181 *(filed 2026-08-11 while working [[F2-180]] — found by asking who else writes the column the promotion adapter was breaking)* |
| **Module** | `module/incident` (`IncidentService#apply`, `IncidentRequest`) · `pages/incidents/IncidentsPage.tsx` — and the pairing is **the register's own create screen**, not a promotion path |
| **Category** | Two artefacts that must agree with nobody maintaining the agreement — the [[F2-156]] class, with a **frontend** vocabulary on one side and a `CHECK` on the other |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** The incident register is NCA ECC 6.1 / ISO 27001 §6.8 core, and **19 of the 22 categories its own form offers cannot be saved.** Every failure is a 409, and until [[F2-180]] fixed the diagnostic, a 409 that described a foreign key |
| **Measured live, not inferred** | `POST /api/v1/incidents` once per option, as `compliance`, against the running stack: `category` **accepted 3 / 22** (`CYBER`, `INFRASTRUCTURE`, `OTHER`) and **refused 19** — `PRIVACY, APPLICATION, NETWORK, CLOUD, DATA_LOSS, OPS, PHYSICAL, THIRD_PARTY, SUPPLY_CHAIN, BUSINESS_CONTINUITY, DR_FAILOVER, SAFETY, INSIDER_THREAT, HR_VIOLATION, COMPLIANCE, REGULATORY_BREACH, AML_SANCTIONS, FINANCIAL_FRAUD, ETHICS`. `status` **accepted 3 / 6**, refusing `CONTAINED`, `ERADICATED`, `RECOVERED` — the middle of the NIST 800-61 lifecycle the screen is modelled on. All 409. |
| **⚠ Why this is filed and not bundled into F2-180** | Different producer, different blast radius, and — decisively — **a different kind of fix.** F2-180's adapters were writing values *chosen by a developer*, so mapping them is a code change with one right answer. Here the values are *offered to a user by the product*, and the two ways to make the screen honest point opposite ways: **(a) widen the CHECK** to the 22 the UI already offers (a migration on a live register's taxonomy, changing every category-grouped dashboard and report), or **(b) narrow the UI** to the 5 the column accepts (deleting a deliberately-designed taxonomy — the list is grouped Technical / Operational / Compliance with per-value Arabic labels and a comment explaining it). ⚙ The **product intent** is plainly the richer list: the column's five come from V4, the original incident module, and the UI was written later and knowingly. That is an argument for (a) — and *which taxonomy governs incident categorisation* is a governance decision about a regulated register, not a casing bug. Same reason [[F2-179]] was filed rather than folded in. |
| **⚠ Do not "fix" it by removing the CHECK** | A closed vocabulary on a register's category is worth having; the defect is that **two** vocabularies exist and the narrower one is invisible from where the choice is made. Whichever way it is resolved, the outcome must be **one** list — and, following F2-180's own lesson, a writer that clamps to it rather than a caller trusted to send legal values. |
| **⚠ The heuristic that found it was wrong, and the finding is only what survived** | A sweep pairing every UI option-list to every constrained column by value overlap produced 30+ candidates and was **discarded** — it paired `VALID_NDI_TABS` with `ck_change_risk` on the strength of `CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW`. Only two pairings are claimed here, both from `IncidentsPage.tsx` to `cyber.incidents`, both **proven with a live POST**. There may well be more instances of this class elsewhere; **this row does not claim to have found them**, and a value-overlap heuristic is not the way to. |
| **Status** | ⬜ **OPEN** — measured, reproduced live, both fixes scoped and costed. Carries one owner decision (widen the taxonomy or narrow the screen). |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **Ask who else writes the column.** F2-180 was scoped to promotion adapters and the adapter turned out to be the *second* writer of `cyber.incidents.category`; the first is the register's own screen, and it is worse off. A finding scoped to one producer should always ask what the other producers of the same column do — the scoping that makes an investigation tractable is also what hides its neighbour. |

## F2-183 · A vocabulary with no CHECK constraint at all, narrowed silently by a case-sensitive Java switch

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-183 *(filed 2026-08-11 while working [[F2-179]] — found by grepping for `safe*`, the naming pattern F2-179's own comment had just called "the tell")* |
| **Module** | `module/consumer/complaints` (`ComplaintService#safeChannel`, `#safeSeverity`) |
| **Category** | The [[F2-179]] family with the mechanism inverted: not a case-insensitive CHECK behind a case-sensitive comparison, but **no CHECK whatsoever**, with the only vocabulary enforcement being a Java `switch` that substitutes rather than refuses |
| **Severity** | **P2** — *raised from the filed P3 on measurement.* Not because the two named columns are worse than described, but because the filing **named the wrong column as the regulatory risk** and missed the one that carries it. See the two corrections below. |
| **What is wrong** | `safeChannel` maps anything outside `{WEB, EMAIL, PHONE, BRANCH, SAMA_REFERRAL, SOCIAL_MEDIA}` to **`WEB`**, and `safeSeverity` maps anything outside `{LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL}` to **`MEDIUM`** — both with a case-**sensitive** `switch`. So `channel: "email"` is stored as **`WEB`** and `severity: "critical"` as **`MEDIUM`**, silently. Measured: the **entire `consumer` schema** has **zero** check constraints — not a subset like [[F2-153]]'s 32, all of them — so the database accepts any string and the substitution is the *only* thing narrowing it. |
| **Why it is worse than it looks, and why it is not just F2-179 again** | The columns are ungoverned, so there are two defects rather than one: the casing bug **and** the absence of the constraint that would have made the casing bug detectable. |
| **⚠⚠ CORRECTION 1 — the harm this row claimed for `channel` does not exist, and the column that does carry it is one the row never mentions** | This filing said a mis-recorded channel *"misstates a regulatory aggregate"* because SAMA asks for volumes **by channel**. **`generateQuarterlyReport` does not aggregate by channel at all** — `ComplaintAggregateReport` has no channel field; it holds totals, SLA-breach percentages, compensation, and **`top_category` / `top_category_count`**. So the channel defect is real and its stated consequence was not: it damages the operational record and the frontend's `CHANNEL_LABEL` lookup, not a report. Meanwhile **`category`** — which this row does not mention — is written **straight from the request body with only `@NotBlank`**, on the **anonymous public endpoint that is the only path that creates a complaint**, into a `NOT NULL NVARCHAR(64)` with no constraint. 🔑 **A filing can be right that something is broken and wrong about why it matters — and the "why" is what sets the severity.** |
| **⚠⚠ And `category` is the sharper defect because the mismatch selects a different ANSWER, not a wrong value** | `generateQuarterlyReport` does `byCategory.merge(c.getCategory(), 1L, Long::sum)` into a `HashMap`, which is case-**sensitive**, then reports the largest bucket to SAMA as `topCategory`. Three complaints in one category submitted in three casings were **three buckets of 1**, so a rival category with 2 won outright — the regulator is told the wrong category is the most complained-about, with the wrong count. The [[F2-182]] KRI-inversion shape one layer up: with an aggregate, a vocabulary mismatch does not degrade to a default, it changes the answer. Pinned by `ComplaintVocabularyTest.aCaseVariantCategoryDoesNotSplitTheSamaReportBucket`. |
| **⚙ Two more columns in the same state, and two deliberately left open** | `customer_id_type` (`NATIONAL_ID \| IQAMA \| PASSPORT \| CR`) was also a straight pass-through. `status`, `update_type`, `from_status`, `to_status` and the report's `top_category` had no constraint either, but their **writers were already closed** — a literal plus `guardTransition`, and literals — so they needed only the CHECK. `subcategory` and `root_cause_code` are **left unconstrained on purpose**: no vocabulary is declared for them anywhere (not the entity, not V199's header, not `lib/complaints.ts`), and dev holds 5 distinct free-text root causes, so inventing one would be a product decision wearing a fix's clothes. Asserted as a decision by `theTwoUnconstrainedColumnsHaveNoDeclaredVocabularyToMirror` rather than left as an absence. |
| **⚠⚠ CORRECTION 2 — the decision this row flagged had already been answered by the data; and the rule it needed is the opposite of the one it stated** | The row said the migration's decision was *what to do about existing rows*, warning that a substituted `channel` is unrecoverable. Measured in **both** real databases before writing a line of SQL: dev **and** prod each hold 12 complaints / 28 timeline rows / 1 report, with **0 values outside any vocabulary and 0 non-canonical casings** — dev's 12 are V199 seed rows inserted by the migration, never through the substituting service. So there is nothing to backfill and nothing unrecoverable. ⚠ The decision that actually mattered is one this row did not raise: **a CHECK on a column whose writer is still open converts today's silently-stored junk into a constraint violation** — here, a **lost complaint on a SAMA-mandated anonymous intake channel**, strictly worse than the defect. 🔑 **Scope the migration to the writers you close in the same commit, not to the columns you can see.** |
| **The fix** | **V375** adds **9** CHECK constraints (the `consumer` schema's first of any kind), and the same commit closes the four open writers with `ClosedVocabulary`: `coerce` for `channel`→`WEB`, `category`→`OTHER`, `severity`→`MEDIUM`, and a new **`coerceOrNull`** for the nullable `customer_id_type`. `coerce` throughout, never `require`: [[F2-182]]'s mechanical rule says a coercion already existed upstream here (the `switch`'s default arm), so out-of-vocabulary values succeed today and refusing them would break working submissions — the line [[F2-179]] drew on the whistleblower portal. `OTHER` is not a guess: it is the taxonomy's own unclassified code. V375 also **normalises casing** before adding the constraints, because the CI collation means the CHECK *accepts* `'critical'` — proved live, Leg 7 — so the constraint alone would have left the defect in place while appearing to guard it. |
| **⚙ The `coerceOrNull` decision** | A nullable closed column has **no in-vocabulary fallback**: nothing in `{NATIONAL_ID, IQAMA, PASSPORT, CR}` means "not stated", so `coerce` has nothing legal to take and picking one would assert an identity document the customer never claimed. `require` would 400 the complaint away. Hence a fourth method on the primitive rather than a hand-rolled ternary at the call site — the shape recurs on every nullable closed column, and hand-rolling is what this whole family exists to stop. Two of its tests assert it can never invent a member. |
| **Gates** | `ClosedVocabularyPinTest` picks up all six new vocabularies automatically and checks them against V375's SQL by reflection; the six constraint names were added to `MUST_BE_FOUND` **because without them the test passes over V375 whether it read it or not** — the anti-vacuity concern that test's own javadoc raises. · `ComplaintVocabularyTest` (20) — behaviour, because the pin proves the Java sets equal the CHECKs and cannot prove the service *consults* them, which is exactly the `safeRole` decoy shape. Includes `theStateMachineAndTheColumnAgreeInBothDirections` (the state machine and `CK_complaint_status` are two independent lists that until now had nothing to agree with) and `theConstraintsThatShareAVocabularyAgreeWithIt` (V375 writes the status vocabulary three times and the pin can only see the one a `ClosedVocabulary` names). |
| **Live verification (19/19, dev)** | V375 applied through pyodbc, **twice**, per house convention. The interesting leg is that the casing-normalisation UPDATEs touch **0 rows** in both real databases, so applying the file as-is would leave that half unexercised — the script therefore **seeds a deliberately lower-case `[REVIEW-TEST]` complaint first** so the UPDATE has something to do, and proves it was normalised before the constraints went on. Then: 9 constraints present, **all trusted** (no `WITH NOCHECK`), none disabled; second application a clean no-op; 7 junk values refused one per constrained column; **Leg 7 — `severity = 'critical'` still ACCEPTED and stored verbatim**, which is the whole argument for closing the writer; cleanup by `CHARINDEX`, back to 12 rows. |
| **⚙ Two harness bugs, both mine** | `ROWVERSION` columns refuse an explicit value, so building the seed INSERT's column list from `sys.columns` had to exclude by **type** (`timestamp`), not by name. And the first draft of the SAMA-report test used a **2-versus-2 tie**, which passed or failed by `HashMap` iteration order — that is not a flaky test, it is a real pre-existing defect the test tripped over, filed as **[[F2-186]]**. Rebuilt as 3-versus-2 so the correct answer is unambiguous. 🔑 **A test that depends on a tie-break nobody chose is asserting the implementation, not the requirement.** |
| **Effort** | M (1 primitive method, 4 writers closed, 2 `safe*` helpers deleted, **1 migration (V375)**, 1 new test class, 2 test classes extended, 19 live legs, **0 frontend change** — `lib/complaints.ts` already declared all five vocabularies correctly as TypeScript unions, which is what made the three-way drift invisible) |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-11.** `consumer` schema CHECK constraints **0 → 9**; open vocabulary writers on the complaint intake **4 → 0**. Two corrections to this row's own filing recorded above, both in the direction of understating what was wrong. Filed on the way out: **[[F2-186]]** (the SAMA report's arbitrary tie-break). |

## F2-184 · Bean-validation constraints on classes no endpoint binds — 20 of them, and the worst was on the only route that creates a sanctions entry

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-184 *(filed 2026-08-11 while working [[F2-182]], whose calendar site was the first confirmed instance; **measured and closed the same day**)* |
| **Module** | `aml/sanctions`, `bcm`, `iam/governance`, `admin/committee`, `platform/export`, `platform/calendar`, `platform/push` (8 fixed) + 10 deferred across `compliance`, `cyber`, `privacy`, `risk`, `tprm` |
| **Category** | An artefact whose position claims a check its behaviour does not perform — the `safeRole(role){return role;}` family ([[F2-175]], [[F2-179]]), but the tell is **structural** rather than lexical |
| **Severity** | **P2** — graded only after measuring, and the grade comes from one site: an unvalidated bulk import into `aml.sanctions_list_entry`, a table with **zero** CHECK constraints, on the **only** route that creates sanctions entries. Filed as "plausibly P3" from the single fail-closed calendar instance; the population contained something worse. 🔑 **An unmeasured population cannot be graded, and guessing low is not the safe direction.** |
| **The measurement (reflection, as the filing prescribed)** | **2,941 types** under `com.tss.grc` including nested ones · **254 controllers**, **2,210 handlers** (matches `LazyEntitySerialisationInvariantTest` exactly, which cross-checks the walk) · **399** body-bound roots marked `@Valid`, **409** after closing over `@Valid` fields and superclasses · **405** types declare a `jakarta.validation.constraints.*` or `@Constraint` annotation · **20 of them are validated by nothing**. Against the **75** the abandoned regex claimed. Every ambiguity resolves toward *treat as validated* — a generic body parameter counts all its type arguments, a `@Valid` field cascades through generics, and the whole superclass chain rides along — so anything reported has survived all of it. |
