The remedy that worked is neither a better regex nor a stripper but **a matcher scoped to the element it judges**, where surrounding prose cannot reach. **(2)** The element-local version then read every button as alive, because `<Button(\s[^>]*?)>` cannot capture JSX attributes: the `>` in `=>` truncates them, so an inline arrow handler was invisible. Both were caught by mutation and neither by reading. |
| **⚠ A third thing only the browser showed: the row-summary formatter was fixture-shaped** | The inbox headline handled 5 of 26 kinds and dumped raw JSON for the rest — and those 5 are **exactly** the kinds the deleted `SEED_INTAKE` fixture contained. It had been written to make the fabricated rows read well, and nothing else could reach the list, so the fallback was unreachable in practice. The first real submission filed in the browser — a GOSI workplace-injury notification — rendered as `{"summary":"…","category":"PHISHING","obser`. ⚙ **A fixture-shaped code path is invisible while the fixture is the only input.** |
| **⚠ The contract test measured its own fixture** | Its port scan is a classpath scan for `RegisterPromotionPort`, and the file's own `FakePort` sits in that very package — so the first run instantiated the fixture with nulls and reported `target()=null` as a shipped adapter. Filtered to `@Component`. Another instance of *the matcher was looking at the wrong span* ([[F2-137]], [[F2-165]], [[F2-171]]), in a newer disguise: the wrong **classpath**, not the wrong text. |
| **➕ An existing guard caught a real design question** | `ChangeModuleBoundaryTest` refused the change adapter: ADR-012 forbids `module/change_mgmt` importing any peer, so a `change_mgmt/intake` adapter is illegal — and `module/intake` cannot hold it either, because Base must not depend on a SKU. `module/change_adapters` is the only place both halves are legal. Its peer list went 5 → 6 **with the reason recorded**, including that this entry is the one that points the *other* way: the five existing adapters implement change's outbound ports, this one implements intake's. |
| **The retirement, and why it is a deletion** | With promotion persisting there is nothing left for the placeholder machinery to guard, so `promotedRecords.ts`, `promotedAdapters.ts`, the merges on **10 register pages** and the **15 inert row-action sites** are gone rather than disabled — a module still exporting `addPromoted` invites the next feature to call it, and the whole defect was one call site away from correct. **Proven before removing, not after:** a promoted DPIA comes back from `GET /api/v1/privacy/dpias` (live-probed, id in the list). The provenance badge survives, re-pointed at the intake row's own `promoted_to_record_id` — it now states a fact instead of reading a cache, and degrades to *no badge* rather than a wrong one when the caller lacks `INTAKE:READ`. |
| **⚠ `assertNotPlaceholder` is KEPT, and that is a deliberate divergence from the filing** | F2-172 was filed asking for it to be removed *"once promotion persists"*, and its population is indeed now empty. It stays because it is an **invariant, not a ceiling**: every id this platform issues is a SQL Server IDENTITY or a UUID, so "a negative integer path segment" is unreachable by construction and free to assert. A ceiling tolerating a population has to go with the population; a total assertion at the one choke point every call passes through costs a regex and turns the next accidental placeholder scheme into a named error rather than an unexplained 404 — which is exactly how F2-171's harms presented. Its javadoc and user-facing message were rewritten, because the old ones cited a mechanism that no longer exists. |
| **⚠ A guard had gone VACUOUS rather than red, which is the quieter half of this defect family** | `publicPortalBackedByServer`'s premise test asserted *"lib/intake really does make zero network calls"* — by grepping for `fetch(`, `api.get` and `axios`. The new calls go through the `intakeApi` client, so **it kept passing while being false**. A premise test that cannot notice its own premise changing is the same defect as the code it guards. Inverted to assert the property that now holds: `lib/intake` must reach the server and must hold no submission store of its own. |
| **⚠ Two assertions failed against source they should have matched** | They were written against a Python probe that matched and failed in vitest against the same source. Cause: `core.autocrlf` gives this checkout `\r\n`, `readFileSync(f,'utf8')` hands them through verbatim, and Python's `read_text()` translates them — so any multi-line anchor agrees in one language and not the other. It surfaced loudly here (*"this moved"* when nothing moved); the quiet version of the same bug is an assertion that silently never matches, which is [[F2-169]]'s vacuous `.not.toMatch`. |
| **Live probe (27/27 + 16/16)** | `ranalyst` — a persona holding **zero** INTAKE permissions — POSTs a SECURITY_INCIDENT and gets **201**, with `submitter_user_id = 5` and `assigned_to = CSIRT`; claiming anonymity on that kind is **refused** and the caller still bound; a SPEAKUP claim is honoured with `uid/name/email/phone` all NULL; all **10** formerly-rejected kinds accepted, WORKPLACE_INJURY minting `WI-…` rather than the `II` fallback; `ranalyst` gets **403** on the inbox and on `GET /{id}`; the unauthenticated tracker answers 200 with exactly `[acknowledgedAt, kind, referenceCode, slaDueAt, status]` and 404 for an unknown code. Then, on the promotion half: promote → 200 and **the DPIA the server named exists in `privacy.dpia`** with the submitted activity name, an Arabic title that is Arabic rather than a copy of the English, `DRAFT`, and the caller's org; the history note names the created record; second promotion → 409; `CONTROL_TEST` → 409 naming the gap **and the refused submission is not marked promoted**; DSR `due_date = received_at + 30 days` with `received_at` equal to the intake acknowledgement to the second. Probe rows tagged `[REVIEW-TEST]`, deleted with `CHARINDEX`, table returned to 0 rows. |
| **Browser, signed in as `compliance`** | The inbox showed **2 real submissions and none of the 5 seeds**; Promote issued `PUT /api/v1/intake/41/triage → 200`; the DPIA rendered on `/privacy?tab=dpia` with a live `/dpias/12` link, and `POST /dpias/12/submit-for-review → 200` moved it to **IN REVIEW** — the governance chain F2-171 said could not proceed. **Negative control:** all six pre-existing DPIAs unchanged. |
| **⚠ Not proven live** | **(a) Cross-tenant isolation.** Dev has 3 organisations but **all 7 users sit in org 1**, so there is no second-tenant login to probe with. The service filters `findById` on `TenantContext` for `findOne` and `triage`, and `list` is org-scoped in the repository — read from the code, not measured. **(b) The target-permission gate**, for the same measurement that justified the rule: no dev persona holds `INTAKE:TRIAGE` without also holding all eight target permissions, so producing a live 403 would mean revoking a grant from the shared dev database. Both stated rather than faked. |
| **⚠ Not attributed: three committed rows vanished between two measurements** | Rows 27–29, created through the API and confirmed by `GET /{id}`, were gone minutes later with `IDENT_CURRENT` at 38 — nine identity values consumed and unaccounted for. No `IntakeRecord` row in `platform.audit_log`, no scheduled sweep anywhere in `module/intake`, and the probe's `CHARINDEX` cleanup keys on a tag those payloads did not carry. Most likely [[F2-74]]'s recorded hazard — a sibling process on the shared dev `TSS_GRC`. **Stated rather than explained**; it did not affect any verified property. |
| **⚠⚠ The two halves were built independently and met in a merge — and that is the last lesson** | The front-door half landed on `master`; the promotion half was still on its branch, both filed under F2-172 on the same day. Git found **10 conflicting files**; the ones that mattered were not textual. Two generated catalogues (`IntakeKindRouting` and `IntakeCatalog`) that git would have kept **both** of, since they are different files — reconciled to one, extended with the titles the adapters need. Two tests whose *premise* the other half falsified: `thePromotionNoteSaysTheTargetDoesNotExistYet` asserted the honest thing to say while nothing created the row, and became false the moment something did. And an entry in `KNOWN_DARK` for `intakeApi.track`, correct when written and wrong once the other half wired the case tracker — caught because that ratchet fails on a **decrease** too. ⚙ **When two slices close the same finding from different ends, the merge conflicts are the least of it: what needs re-deciding is every claim each side made about what was still missing.** |
| **Effort** | XL (1 SPI package, 13 adapters across 11 modules, 1 catalogue, V374, 7 test classes, ~70 assertions, 41 mutations, 43 live probes, 2 browser verifications, 10 register pages retired, 1 two-way merge) |
| **Filed** | **F2-173** (prefix `CR` is shared by `CHANGE_REQUEST` and `CR_ANNUAL_CONFIRMATION`, so a submitter cannot tell the two tracking codes apart — ceilinged at exactly one collision) · **F2-174** (`assigned_to` holds stakeholder codes like `TPRM_LEAD` and `CSIRT` that resolve to no role and nothing routes on, the F2-94 recipient-key class one table over) · **F2-175** (`MlModelDriftService#openCriticalDriftIssue` is a second writer to `intake.intake_records` bypassing `IntakeService`) · **F2-176** (six `CONTROL_TEST` kinds have no register to be promoted into, and now fail with a 409 naming the gap — a functional regression against the fabricated behaviour they had, taken deliberately). |
| **Residue** | `/portal/dsr` remains blocked by [[F2-138]] — no anonymous intake endpoint exists, so a data subject is refused. What changed is that the page now **shows** the refusal (bilingual, naming the PDPL right and directing them to the DPO) instead of writing to `localStorage` and issuing a reference code; it posts to the real endpoint with `anonymous: true` so it starts working by itself when F2-138 lands. |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **"Implemented on neither side" is a state two half-built implementations produce and neither reveals.** The client minted an id and the server accepted one; each looked like the other end's job was done, and the only artefact was a history note quoting a number. ⚙ **Measure what a rewire will hit before writing it** — three of the four defects here would have shipped as regressions from a mechanical repointing, and two carry statutory clocks. ⚙ And the corollary this slice added to the fabrication family: **when the cause is removed, check the guards that were written for it — a premise that silently stops holding is worse than a guard that fails.** |

## F2-171 · Intake promotion writes the register row to `localStorage`, with a positive id, and eleven registers render live governance buttons on it

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-171 *(opened 2026-08-09 out of [[F2-170]]'s triage residue — "16 entities no screen can create" — by reading the service instead of the client)* |
| **Module** | Platform-wide: `lib/intake`, `lib/promotedRecords`, `lib/promotedAdapters` → 11 register pages (privacy, risk, incidents, TPRM, ethics, change, BCM, compliance ×2, CAPA) |
| **Category** | Fabricated data substituting for a server write — undisclosed, **and acted upon** |
| **Severity** | **P2 High** — certain harms on every promotion; the wrong-record harm is rare but grows with tenant size |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09** — `promotedIntakeSafety.test.ts`, 14 tests, mutation **11/12** (the 12th is a stated limit), live-probed + browser-verified. FE suite 473/473 in 49 files |
| **How it was found** | F2-170's residue listed `dpiaApi.create` as a dark method and I filed "16 entities cannot be created" as capability backlog. The **root cause is not a missing button.** `PrivacyPage.tsx:323` reads *"DD-76: route DSR / breach / DPIA creation through Services Center"* — creation is **deliberately** routed to intake, and `dpiaApi.create` is dark **because that other path exists**. Following it is what produced this finding: the other path does not write to the server |
| **What promotion actually does** | `intake.ts`'s `triage(…, 'PROMOTE', …)` calls `addPromoted()`, which writes to `localStorage['grc.promotedRecords']` **and nothing else**. No `privacy.dpia` / `risk.risks` / `incident.incidents` row is created. The row is invisible to every other user and machine, and clearing site data destroys it. The intake record's permanent history note reads *"Promoted to DPIA #482913"* — naming a record that does not exist |
| **⚠ The server side was already built** | `module/intake` has `IntakeController` + `IntakeService` (DD-82) with submit / list / triage / public-tracker, and `intake.intake_records.promoted_to_record_id`. **No product code calls `/api/v1/intake`** — one mention exists, in a test's comment. Live-probed: `GET /api/v1/intake` → **200, totalElements 0**; the table exists and holds **0 rows**; `PUT /api/v1/intake/999999/triage` → a correct 404 ProblemDetail. So the capability is implemented, reachable, and has never been used. `IntakeService`'s own javadoc says it *"Implements the same … lifecycle the React useIntake() hook drives"* — nothing drives it |
| **🔑 Three files, three accounts of one value** | `promotedAdapters.ts` opened with *"Promoted records use **negative** synthesized ids … so they never collide with backend-assigned ids"*. `PromotedRecord.id` was documented *"highest existing + 1"*. `intake.ts` actually minted **`Date.now() % 1_000_000`** — a **positive** integer in exactly the range SQL Server IDENTITY values occupy. Every one of the twelve numeric adapters then passed it through with `typeof p.id === 'number' ? p.id : Number(p.id)`. **The file that documented the hazard was the file that let it through** — [[F2-168]]'s shape precisely, where `entityAnchors.ts` opened with the mock-id range and the bug lived at the call site. Exactly **one of thirteen** adapters honoured the contract: `toCapaFromObservation`, which mints a string |
| **The harms, ordered by certainty** | **(1) Certain, every promotion:** nothing is persisted; the promotion is a fiction with an audit note. **(2) Certain:** the row renders the same live actions as a server row — Approve/Submit/Reject/Expire a DPIA, advance an incident phase, close a risk, delete a vendor — each addressing an id the server never issued, so the governance chain cannot proceed. **(3) Certain:** the title was a `<Link to={/dpias/:id}>` to a nonexistent record. **(4) Rare but scaling:** measured in dev, **0.056% of promotions** would name *some* real record across the eleven registers (Σ max(id) ÷ 1,000,000 = 560/1e6), and that share grows linearly with every row a tenant adds — on such a promotion `dpiaApi.approve(d.id)` approved a **real, unrelated** DPIA while the screen showed the promoted row's title |
| **⚠ Why five existing guards were all green** | [[F2-137]] asks whether a route backed by `lib/intake` is **public** — its scope is the `/portal/` and `/public/` prefixes, and this path is entirely authenticated (a signed-in DPO presses New → DPIA and a triager promotes it). Its premise test, *"lib/intake really does make zero network calls"*, is what proves the substrate is still client-only — it measured the fact and its scope excluded the consequence. [[F2-167]] disabled actions on fabricated rows but resolves on the **demo** flag (`isDemo`/`demoMode`/`showingDemo`); a promoted row is not demo, so `disabled` was false for it. `demoFallbackContract` matches `/mock/i` in the import path, and this store is named after the domain it fakes. [[F2-168]]/[[F2-169]] swept the mock corpus, which this is not part of. **A fourth source of fabricated rows that no fabrication guard measured** |
| **Fix — two layers, and only one of them is the control** | **(a) Structural:** `assertNotPlaceholder()` at all **three** network entry points in `lib/api.ts` (`request`, `downloadFile`, `uploadFile`) refuses a negative-id path segment before `fetch`, throwing an `ApiError(0, …)` that names the cause. Total and un-forgettable: whatever a page misses, the request cannot leave. **(b) UX:** `mintPromotedId()` is negative by construction (a negative id cannot name a SQL Server IDENTITY row **ever** — the property bought is not "collision unlikely"); `promotedId()` **coerces on read** with `-Math.abs(n)`, because overlays minted before this fix sit in users' browsers and localStorage has no migration step; `isUnsyncedId()` is a total predicate, so the 15 row-action sites need no page flag; the DPIA tab drops its `<Link>` and shows a **"Not saved"** badge instead of a fabricated `#id` |
| **Verified live** | Seeded one promoted DPIA through the real overlay in the browser, signed in as `admin`: the row rendered `disabled: true` on both PDPL workflow buttons with the Arabic reason on each, `links: []`, and the **"غير محفوظ"** badge — while all **six real DPIAs on the same screen** kept `/dpias/1…6` and live buttons. A guard that disabled everything would have looked identical without that negative control. Server-side: `POST /dpias/-1754000000000/approve` → **404 "Resource Not Found: DPIA"**, which is the bare, unexplained failure a user used to get |
| **⚠ Two of my own assertions shipped vacuous before mutation caught them** | The query-string test used `?delta=-5&sort=-id` — no value is preceded by a slash, so it passed whether or not the query was stripped, asserting its named property only by coincidence. The second attempt, `?filter=/-5&sort=-id`, **also** passed: the segment matcher needs `/` or end-of-string after the digits and `&` is neither. Only `?sort=-id&filter=/-5` distinguishes the implementations. Separately the source scan tested `/isUnsyncedId/.test(src)`, which the *import line* satisfies — so the regression a reviewer would actually make (editing the condition, keeping the import) passed clean; it is now anchored inside `disabled={…}`. Third occurrence of "the matcher was looking at the wrong span of text" ([[F2-137]], [[F2-165]]) |
| **⚠ And my own harness misreported 11 of 12 mutations** | The runner's `Tests N failed` line is ANSI-coloured, so `/Tests\s+\d+ failed/` never matched and every mutation printed **MISSED** over a visible `FAIL`. A harness that misreports is worse than none — it would have sent a genuinely unguarded assertion to the register as proven. Same class as the `nohup` wrapper exiting 0 over a dead application |
| **Stated limit, measured not assumed** | The source scan resolves **per file**, so a page with several action sites passes on the strength of any one. Mutation confirms it: replacing `PrivacyPage`'s `const unsynced = isUnsyncedId(d.id)` with `false` leaves it green, because that file's DSR and breach tables still carry inline guards. Accepted rather than fixed, because layer (a) is the enforced property; recorded in the test itself so nobody reads the pass as coverage |
| **Effort** | M (4 lib files, 8 pages, 1 test file of 14 assertions, 12 mutations, 1 live probe, 1 browser verification) |
| **Follow-up filed** | **[[F2-172]] — ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-09.** The intake record itself now persists server-side (submit / list / triage / one-record read), and the rewire found two defects that would have shipped as regressions had the client simply been repointed: the server accepted **16 of the 26** intake kinds, and `POST /api/v1/intake` was held by **3 of 69 roles, all administrators**. ⚠ The *second* half is still open and unchanged: nothing creates the downstream register row on either side, so `promoted_to_record_id` is NULL by design and the placeholder machinery this finding shipped stays in place until an adapter per target module exists. [[F2-138]]'s anonymous-DSR endpoint stays owner-blocked and gates the public half |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **"Nothing can create X" is a statement about the code you have not read yet.** F2-170 filed this as capability backlog on the strength of reading one service, and the classification was right — but the *reason* was wrong, and the real reason was a P2. The client told me the create method was uncalled; only the page comment said creation had been deliberately re-routed, and only following that route showed where it went. ⚙ Corollary for the fabrication family: **five guards can be green because each measured a different property of the same defect class.** When a new source of fabricated rows appears, ask which existing guard's *scope* excludes it — not whether one exists |

## F2-162 — The register contradicted itself: one finding filed twice with opposite states, one closed as collateral still reading OPEN

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-162 *(found 2026-08-08 while answering "what remains in the plan" — the answer was meant to be a report, and measuring it found the instrument wrong)* |
| **Category** | Programme integrity — the register is the flat per-finding record, outlives the plan, and is what an external auditor is handed |
| **Severity** | **P3** — no code defect. The harm is that the two documents this programme plans against disagreed, in the direction that **overstates what remains**: a reader would have re-done V361's work and re-opened `sharia`'s guards |
| **Current State** | ✔ **CLOSED 2026-08-08.** Four cells corrected and `FindingsRegisterConsistencyTest` added (5 checks, **8/8 mutation**, 2 of the 8 asserting the gate does *not* fire) |
| **The measurement** | 146 rows parsed by heading, each row's state read from its own block. **1 duplicated id** (`F2-45`, two rows, `⬜ OPEN` vs `✅ CLOSED`) · **1 row with no state field at all** (`F2-131`, withdrawn, disposition in the heading only) · **2 cells contradicted by evidence elsewhere in the repo** (`F2-120`, `F2-146`) |
| **🔑 Why `F2-127` was updated and `F2-120` was not — the transferable half** | Both were closed by the same slice, F2-145(e). `F2-127` is `openbanking`'s row and that slice was *named* after the module, so its row was visited. `F2-120` is `sharia`'s, closed as **collateral** — F2-145's own cell records *"`sharia` FULLY CLOSED … and with it [[F2-120]]"* — and nothing visited it. ⚙ **A finding closed as a side effect is the one nobody updates**, and the claim that it closed is sitting in another row where a mechanical check can read it |
| **⚠ The witness that was measured and REJECTED** | The obvious third rule — *a packaged migration whose header names `F2-nnn` closes it* — would have caught `F2-146` (V361's header names it). It is **not** a rule, because `V359`'s header names `F2-130` while fixing `F2-81`: it cites F2-130's *shape* ("a permission nobody holds") as the reason for its own design, and F2-130 is genuinely open. **Naming a finding is not a claim to close it.** A rule that invents defects gets switched off and takes the true findings with it |
| **⚠ So state what the gate cannot see** | It could not have caught `F2-146` — remedy shipped, both the register and the plan kept reading `OPEN`, and **neither document contradicted the other because both were stale**. Nor is "the plan and the register must agree" available: the plan tracks findings in more than one shape (78 of 140 ids in row shape), so a plan-side state extractor would report disagreements that are not there |
| **⚠ A mutant survived the first version of the rule, and the reason generalises** | The natural definition — *open if the cell carries an open marker and no closed marker* — left the gate **green** when `F2-120` was reverted to `🔴 OPEN`, because the rest of that cell narrates its own closure and contains the word *shipped*. A state cell here is mostly prose, so any-marker matching reads "mentions a closure" as "is closed". Fixed by **position**: the first disposition marker in the cell is the state. ➕ That is also the more honest reading — it moves 7 rows from closed to open (`F2-30`, `F2-33`, `F2-112`, `F2-115`, `F2-133`, `F2-141`, `F2-148`), every one a `🟡`/`🔶` row whose leading marker says *partly* |
| **⚠ Two row schemas, pinned rather than unified** | **62** rows carry `**Status**` as the state (the older schema, where `Current State` describes the *defect*); **83** carry `**Current State**` as the state; **60** carry both. A script reading `Current State` as the status silently reads a problem description for 62 rows — which is what this slice's own first pass did, reporting **101 of 146** findings as not-closed. Rewriting 62 rows is a bigger and riskier edit than the defect warrants, so the canonical reading (`Status` wins) is pinned in the test where every future scan can read it |
| **Fix** | `F2-120` → closed by F2-145(e)/V367 · `F2-146` → closed by V361, re-verified live (27/27 columns in dev, 13/13 of the `AuditFinding` set) · `F2-131` → state cell added · `F2-45` → consolidated into one row, keeping the three things the filed row said that the worked row did not · plan-side: `RC-A`, `F2-77` and `F2-146` status cells corrected |
| **➕ It also corrected the answer this slice was asked for** | The report that started it said *"17 findings open-but-tripwired"* — the tripwired subset. Under one uniform reading the register holds **36 open or partly-open rows** against 145. Neither figure was wrong about its own population; the first was quoted for a question about the whole |
| **References** | `tss-grc-backend/src/test/java/com/tss/grc/config/FindingsRegisterConsistencyTest.java` · sibling of `FindingsRegisterCoverageTest` (plan→register coverage; deliberately not merged — a ratchet answering two questions reports one number and hides whichever half is failing) · [[F2-45]] · [[F2-120]] · [[F2-130]] · [[F2-131]] · [[F2-146]] |
| **Lesson** | **This programme has an instrument for baselines going stale and had none for the register that records the findings.** `MeasuredBaselineFreshnessTest` gates the measured numbers, `GovernanceDocumentIntegrityTest` gates the HISTORIC stamps, `ModuleRegistryContractTest` gates the module count — and the document an auditor is actually handed could contradict itself for a day with a green build. ⚙ **The gap is always the artefact nobody thinks of as code** |

## F2-161 · The exercise runtime was platform-administrator-only, and the person facilitating the exercise could only watch

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-161 *(measured 2026-08-08, the second consumer of [[F2-159]]'s ownership mechanism)* |
| **Category** | Authorisation / **a ghost role name plus an unpopulated real one**, on the path a business-continuity tool is used from during a live exercise |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** `ExerciseRuntimeController`'s write guards were `hasAnyRole('FACILITATOR','BCM_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN')`. `FACILITATOR` matches no row in `iam.roles` and **`BCM_MANAGER` has 0 users**, so dispatching an inject, adding an on-the-fly inject, transitioning the run and assigning or removing an observer were reachable by the **platform administrator and nobody else**. ⚠ This is worse than [[F2-159]]'s model case in one specific way: the model register is read at leisure, and this is the screen someone is on **while the exercise clock runs** |
| **Provenance** | Not sought — it is the item [[F2-159]] named as next, on the strength of `bcm.exercise_run.facilitator_user_id` being populated **4/4**. The 0-user `BCM_MANAGER` half was not predicted and only appears when you ask who actually holds the surviving names |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-08.** `ExerciseRunOwnershipResolver` (one new class — the registry made the second consumer cheap) plus **15** guard conversions: 6 on `ExerciseRuntimeController` (`#id`) and 9 on `ExerciseObserverController` (`#runId`, where every route names a run). Ghost role names **4 → 3**; pure role sites **425 → 410**. All four dev runs are facilitated by `rmanager`, who could read them (RISK_MANAGER is on the read guards) and not drive them; live-proven **201 on `POST /observers`** and a **409 from the service** on `custom-inject` — the guard admits, the business rule refuses a run that has not started |
| **🔑 The converse is proved per record, not per user** | There is no run `rmanager` does *not* facilitate, so the converse could not come from a second row. It was proved by pointing the **same endpoint, same token** at a run whose `facilitator_user_id` was temporarily somebody else: **403**, then restored. That is the property a `FACILITATOR` role could never have had — with a role, the facilitator of run 1 could drive run 4, which during a live exercise is precisely what must not happen |
| **⚠ Three routes cannot be bound, and getting this wrong is a 500 rather than a 403** | `POST /` starts a run that does not exist yet; `GET /` is a collection; `by-exercise/{exerciseId}` is scoped by **exercise** — one exercise has many runs, possibly with different facilitators, so the exercise id cannot answer *"do you facilitate this run"*. The identical wide guard text sat on both bindable and unbindable routes, so the conversion had to be done **per line, not per guard string**: a textual replace would have put `#id` into the expression of a method with no such parameter, and SpEL then throws — **a 500 on the run list**. `ExerciseRunOwnershipGuardTest` pins both directions, including the copied-`#runId`-as-`#id` mistake |
| **Why the observation endpoints are bound too** | Recording, flagging and promoting an observation are findings *about* the exercise its facilitator ran, normally V367's self-review shape. Two measured reasons they are safe: `flagObservationForAar` already enforces authorship **in the service** — *"Only the observation author can change the AAR flag"* — so the guard is a coarse outer gate over a real inner control; and `promoteObservationToGap` creates a tracked `BcmGap`, which is self-incriminating rather than self-serving. `removeObserver` soft-deletes the assignment only and audit-logs it, so it cannot erase a finding |
| **Recommendation** | The **three** remaining ghosts (`AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR`, `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER`, `AUDIT_DIRECTOR`) will **not** fall to this mechanism and that is worth stating plainly: they need *"is the caller a seated member of this committee?"*, and the record being guarded is not the committee — it is a finding or a pivot the committee **reviews**. A `CommitteeSeatResolver` is a different abstraction, not another `EntityOwnershipResolver`, so F2-52's last three are a design decision rather than a copy of this slice |

## F2-154 · A fresh install is 225 role grants short of dev, the chain ORDER is why, and the same folder run twice adds 875

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-154 *(measured 2026-08-07 while closing [[F2-143]]; it is the half F2-143 filed a number for and never looked at)* |
| **Category** | Deployment integrity — the authorisation a customer's tenant administrator gets is not the one dev grants |
| **Severity** | **P1.** `ORG_ADMIN` is the primary tenant administrator and the role [[F2-81]]'s onboarding provisions. On a fresh install it held **30 fewer grants** and could read **none** of BCM, COMPLIANCE, EVIDENCE, SCM, SUST, AI or NDI. `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` could not read compliance. `VIEWER` could read nothing outside RISK and PRIVACY |
| **Current State** | ✔ **CLOSED 2026-08-07 — V372.** Fresh install **1,344 → 1,556** grants against dev's **1,567**; the residue is **exactly 11 and every one of them is deliberate** (8 `PLATFORM_ADMIN`, which `ModulePermissionEvaluator` bypasses in code, and 3 `RISK_ANALYST` writes no migration declares), with **0** in the other direction. Proven on a clean `V1→V372` run over an **empty** database, not on a patched one |
| 🔑 **The mechanism, and it is silent by construction** | Every grant migration in this folder is an `INSERT … SELECT … FROM (VALUES …) JOIN iam.roles JOIN iam.permissions WHERE NOT EXISTS (…)`. A set-based INSERT over a JOIN inserts **nothing** when either side is absent, and `NOT EXISTS` **cannot distinguish *already granted* from *nothing matched***. So a grant whose role or permission row is created later in the chain is dropped with no error, no row and a successful migration. On dev the Python bootstrap had created both sides *before Flyway ever ran*, so the same file granted — which is why the defect exists only on the database nobody had built |
| 🔑 **Proven by replay, not argued — and the number is the finding** | Running the **identical folder a second time** over the already-built database adds **875 grants across 20 migrations**: V284 **+351**, V313 **+81**, V301 **+56**, V248 +39, V239 +29, V271 +29, V320 +14. The same files doing different work depending on when they run. ⚠ **And a second pass is NOT the fix**: it overshoots dev by **686**, because it also re-applies everything V333, V335 and V367–V371 deliberately **revoked**. *Re-running an idempotent folder resurrects revocations* — so per-file idempotency is not set-level idempotency, and the folder has never had the latter |
| 🔑 **The extreme case is a parity rule that is really a snapshot** | V284's own comment says *"EXPORT as a 6th standard action for every module that has READ, with READ-parity default grants (behaviour unchanged until a tenant tightens)"*. It grants `MODULE:EXPORT` to every holder of `MODULE:READ` **at the moment V284 runs**, so every READ granted afterwards (V301, V313, V320, V327…V362) has no EXPORT partner. That is why **78 of the 225 are EXPORT and 0 of them are parity-restorable**: the matching READ is missing too, so the EXPORT loss is *downstream* of the READ loss and fixing EXPORT alone would have restored nothing. ⚠ **A parity migration is a snapshot, not an invariant** |
| **What V372 does, and why it is two lists** | [[F2-143]]'s standing rule is *generate, do not hand-type, and do not copy a database of unknown provenance*. So the rows are generated from the measured diff and **partitioned by authority**: **group A = 188** grants **this folder already declares** (authority: the folder, proven by the replay above), **group B = 26 SCM** grants declared by **no migration anywhere** (authority: dev's persona matrix alone, and the migration says so at the site). Keeping them apart is what lets a later reader re-decide group B without touching group A |
| ➕ **`scm` needed the strongest evidence and got it** | Group B's only authority is dev, so *is it real access?* had to be answered: **68 guards name SCM** (23 READ / 43 WRITE / 2 DELETE), and live through the Vite proxy `so_officer` — which holds no SCM permission — is **403 on all three** probed endpoints while `auditor`, `ranalyst` and `viewer` are **200**. A fresh install's `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` could reach none of the 68. ⚠ `SCM:EXPORT` is granted and named by **no** guard — an instance of [[F2-13b]]'s catalogued-but-unguarded set, kept for parity with dev rather than pruned here |
| 🔑 **And the two auditor roles were EXACTLY BACKWARDS, which is a better reason than the one this row first gave** | A fresh install granted `AUDITOR` — the generic read-only assurance role — `EVIDENCE:WRITE` and `NDI:WRITE`, while `INTERNAL_AUDITOR`, the role that does fieldwork and uploads workpapers, held **neither**, its grants being among the 188 ordering dropped. dev has it the other way round. So group A restores one half and a `DELETE` takes the other, and one inversion is fixed in one file. ⚠ **Do not read that as "the auditor persona loses evidence write"** — measured live, dev's `auditor` **user holds both roles** and keeps it through `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` (201 on `POST /api/v1/evidence/items`). **A role is not a persona when a user holds two of them**, and reading the `AUDITOR` role alone had me briefly filing `CLAUDE.md`'s persona line as wrong when it is correct |
| **The durable half** | `RoleGrantDerivationRatchetTest` — hermetic, no database. Of **108** grant INSERTs in **34** files, exactly **6 in 4 files** derive the `(role, permission)` pair by reading `iam.role_permissions` itself; a 7th fails the build. ⚠ Its tolerated set is a **version→reason map**, not a list, because its first version gave one blanket reason (*"all four are below prod's Flyway head, so they are immutable"*) and **its own third assertion refused it: V346 is ABOVE V344.** V346 is a *transfer* — it moves a grant from a renamed permission onto its replacement, so its population is the holders of a permission that stops existing and there is no later arrival to miss. 🔑 **One reason covering four exceptions is usually one reason covering three and a fourth nobody checked** |
| ⚠ **Why the hazard is documented in the test and not at the three sites** | The obvious remedy — a warning comment at each derived INSERT — **is not available.** V284, V301 and V313 are at or below the deployed server's Flyway head (V344), so editing any of them changes its checksum and the next `flyway:migrate` fails validation before running anything. **A migration applied to production is immutable, so it cannot be annotated with its own defect** |
| ⚠ **What V372's eight THROWs do NOT guarantee** | Flyway runs a migration **once**. They guarantee the state a fresh install *starts* in and nothing after it. Mutation-tested: deleting a group-A grant and re-running V372 **silently repairs** it — correct for a re-run, and exactly why a re-run cannot be the detector. Stated in the file rather than left to be assumed from the word THROW |
| ➕ **Two of the eight assert an absence and two assert its mirror** | The anti-resurrection check (V367/V368/V371's revoked pairs must still be gone) exists because a grant-restoring migration is the obvious way to undo three self-review fixes by accident. And ⚠ **the obvious form of the REGULATOR_VIEWER check was wrong and THROWing on all three databases**: *"holds no EXPORT"* is false, because F2-59/V335 revoked the eleven standing raw-register extracts while F2-60/V333 deliberately left the **governed** `REGULATORY:EXPORT` package. The invariant is *exactly one, and it is that one*, plus a second check that it is still **present** — an absence-only check passes on a database where a supervisory authority can furnish nothing at all, which is D-10b's inverse finding |
| **Verification** | Clean `V1→V372` on an **empty** database: **360 migrations applied**, 471 tables / 51 schemas / 178 FKs, **0** JPA-mapped tables missing. Grants **1,556 / 1,567 / residue 11 / extra 0**. Applied **twice** to the built database and **twice to dev** — 0 rows changed on either second pass, and **0 on dev's first**, so it is a proven no-op there. Backend suite **3,426/0/0**. Live **20/20** through the Vite proxy over 5 personas. **Mutation 11/11 killed**: 8 against the database (5 refused, 3 repaired) and 3 against the source tree. Probe residue **0**, cleaned with `CHARINDEX` |
| ⚠ **Two of my own instruments were wrong first** | **(a)** The derived-grant classifier called **all 108** statements derived, because `FROM iam.role_permissions` appears in nearly every one — inside the `NOT EXISTS` guard. It has to strip parenthesised groups first and ask what the statement's **own** FROM names. **(b)** The ratchet's V372 assertions searched the **raw** file, and a mutant that replaced the ETHICS predicate with `OR (1 = 0)` **survived twice**: first because every name it sought was still in the header paragraph *explaining* the check, then because `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` appears thirteen times in group A's VALUES list. It now matches whole whitespace-normalised **predicates** against comment-stripped SQL. 🔑 **A source-text assertion cannot tell a live predicate from a comment describing it, and a file that documents its guard well is where that failure is invisible** — third instance after [[F2-33]]'s wording ratchet and [[F2-147]]'s sender scan |
| **References** | `V372__fresh_install_role_grants_the_chain_order_silently_dropped.sql` · `RoleGrantDerivationRatchetTest` · `V284__iam_break_glass_export.sql` · `full_chain_proof.py` · `chain_proof.py` · [[F2-143]] · [[F2-153]] · [[F2-146]] · [[F2-81]] · [[F2-23]] · [[F2-13b]] · [[F2-09]] |
| **Lesson** | **An idempotency guard hides an ordering failure, because "nothing to do" and "nothing matched" are the same query result.** [[F2-153]]'s lesson was that `IF NOT EXISTS … CREATE TABLE` discards everything the statement carried; this is its data-side twin, and together they say the same thing about the whole folder: **the migration set was written as a description of dev, and a description read in order is not a history.** ⚠ Method: the finding was invisible until a *complete* chain existed, and the chain became complete four commits earlier for unrelated reasons. **An instrument reaching completeness is itself a reason to re-run every measurement that was blocked on it** |

## F2-155 · The chain-proof instrument could not run at all, and the reason was on the filesystem

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-155 *(hit 2026-08-07 on the first command of the [[F2-143]] slice)* |
| **Category** | Tooling — a committed instrument that hardcodes an assumption about one machine |
| **Severity** | **P3** — no product impact, but it blocked the P1 above on its first statement, and [[F2-143]]'s row names this script as its reproduction recipe |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-07.** `chain_proof.py` now creates its scratch database with explicit files under `<repo>/.chain-proof-data` (`CHAIN_PROOF_DATA_DIR` overrides), so the proof no longer depends on the state of C: — and can run on a build agent whose C: is locked down |
| **The failure** | `CREATE DATABASE TSS_GRC_ChainProof` → *error 5118: the file "C:\Program Files\…\MSSQL\DATA\TSS_GRC_ChainProof.mdf" is compressed but does not reside in a read-only database or filegroup.* The script let SQL Server choose the location; that directory carries the NTFS `Compressed` attribute, and new files inherit it |
| 🔑 **The cause is this programme's own earlier remediation** | The 2026-08-06 disk incident was cleared by freeing ~22 GB **by NTFS-compressing C:**. Existing database files were left uncompressed, so `TSS_GRC` and `TSS_GRC_Deployment` are unaffected and nothing looked wrong — **only NEW databases fail, which is every chain and schema proof.** ⚠ So the fix for one blocker created a second, quieter one, and the second outlived the first: C: has 57 GB free and `CREATE DATABASE` still fails |
| ➕ **The sibling had already solved it and the knowledge did not travel** | `full_chain_proof.py` puts its files on D: **and documents exactly this error in a docstring**. `chain_proof.py`, committed the same day for the same finding, did not. [[F2-134]]'s shape precisely — three scripts hardcoded a Windows path there; here it is a default nobody passed. **Two copies of an instrument diverge on the environment first** |
| **Rejected fix** | `compact /u /s` on the SQL data directory. It would work, and it edits the user's SQL Server installation to work around a script's own default. The same reasoning that rejected `takeown` for the `ApplicationTemp` landmine earlier the same day |
| **Verification** | `chain_proof.py` and `full_chain_proof.py` both build V1→V372 to completion with files on D:. `CLAUDE.md`'s disk landmine now records error 5118 alongside OS error 112, because the two look nothing alike and neither names the disk |
| **References** | `chain_proof.py` · `full_chain_proof.py` · `CLAUDE.md` (landmines) · [[F2-134]] · [[F2-77]] |
| **Lesson** | **Fixing a resource problem can break the same operation a second way, and the second failure will not resemble the first.** OS error 112 says *out of space*; error 5118 says *compressed*; both come out of one `CREATE DATABASE` and neither points at the disk. ⚠ And the transferable rule: **a scratch database must never choose its own path** — name the files, on the volume the repo lives on |

## F2-153 · A fresh install enforces 32 fewer CHECK constraints and 53 fewer foreign keys than dev, and an idempotency guard is why

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-153 *(measured 2026-08-07, extending [[F2-09]]'s convergence diff to constraint bodies)* |
| **Category** | Deployment integrity — the schema a customer gets does not enforce what dev enforces |
| **Severity** | **P1.** `iam.user_roles` and `iam.role_permissions` have **no foreign keys at all** on a fresh install, so a grant can reference a deleted role or a permission that never existed and nothing objects. Value-domain CHECKs are absent across `scm` (11), `bcm`, `risk` and `ethics`, so a fresh install accepts statuses and types the application's own enums do not contain |
| **Current State** | ✔ **CLOSED 2026-08-07 — V364, V365, V366.** Every remaining difference on every measured axis is either a **deliberate exclusion** (an end in [[F2-141]]'s no-code set) or **above the chain's stop**. Closing measurement: CHECK dev 417 / built 414, missing 3 = the 3 excluded · FOREIGN KEY dev 185 / built 178, missing 7 = the 7 excluded · UNIQUE-by-property dev 271 / built 268, missing 3 = the 3 excluded · **extra 0 on all three axes** |
| 🔑 **V366 — and the direction I had not measured is the one that reaches production** | Running the diff the other way round (build **minus** dev) found **five objects the migration set creates and neither dev nor prod had**: `UX_departments_org_code`, `UX_bcp_plans_org_code`, `UX_bia_assessments_org_code`, `UX_bcm_compl_org_req` and `CK_bia_rto_le_mtpd`. **So the running platform allowed two departments with the same code in one organisation**, duplicate BCP plan codes, duplicate BIA codes, a duplicated compliance-requirement mapping, and a BIA whose RTO exceeded its MTPD — while a customer provisioned from the folder was protected from all five. Proven on dev in a rolled-back transaction: a second department with code `'CEO'` in org 1 is **REFUSED naming the index** with it, **ACCEPTED** without. ⚠ **Prod descends from a dev dump, so a gap in the BOOTSTRAP is a gap in the live system, while a gap in the MIGRATIONS only bites a fresh install.** I spent two slices on the less consequential direction because it was the one I had measured |
| ⚠ **And it settles what this row filed as a product question** | The row said `ck_bia_rto_le_mtpd` was *"either dev's data violates RTO ≤ MTPD or the rule is wrong"*. Measured: **dev 7 rows, prod 7 rows, 0 violations, 0 NULLs**, and no migration ever drops it. The rule is right, the data satisfies it, and the constraint is simply absent from the bootstrap — **not a product question at all, a convergence gap in a direction I had not looked**. The four unique indexes stay **filtered** (`WHERE is_deleted = 0`, copied from the built database): unfiltered, they would refuse to re-use the code of a soft-deleted department, turning a correctness fix into a data-entry dead end |
| 🔑 **The FK half is why this row is a P1, demonstrated not argued** | On a fresh install `iam.user_roles` had **no `FK_ur_user` and no `FK_ur_role`**, and `iam.role_permissions` no `FK_rp_role` / `FK_rp_perm` — so the authorisation tables had no referential integrity at all. Proven on the fresh-install database inside a **rolled-back transaction**: a grant naming role `100002`, which does not exist, is **REFUSED and the error names `FK_ur_role`** with the key in place, and **ACCEPTED** with it dropped. Deleting a role left its grants behind, pointing at nothing, and nothing objected |
| ➕ **A third object class, found by auditing the second** | Checking index cover for two FKs showed the "missing index" behind them is a **UNIQUE constraint** — so the index axis is a *correctness* axis. A fresh install lacked **11**, including `iam.users.UQ_username (organisation_id, username)` and `UQ_email`, `iam.roles.UQ_role_name`, `iam.permissions.UQ_permission (module, action)` and `platform.organisations.UQ_org_short_code`. **Two users could share a username inside one tenant**, and `UserRepository.findByUsername` returns an `Optional` — with two matching rows it does not return the right one, it throws or picks arbitrarily. The database constraint was the only control and a fresh install did not have it |
| ⚠ **A false positive I nearly shipped, and the third instrument to need this correction** | Comparing unique indexes **by name** reported 15 missing. One was `UQ__nafath_t__85C600AEA2D5FA14` on `platform.nafath_transaction(transaction_id)` — a **system-generated** name, and dev, prod and the built database each carry that constraint under a *different* generated name. It read as absent while being enforced everywhere. Re-comparing on the **property** (schema, table, ordered columns, filter) gives **14 missing, 11 shippable**. This is the treatment DEFAULT constraints already had on the CHECK axis, which I failed to carry across |
| 🔑 **Why 29 and not 32 — my own gate refused the first draft** | It constrained all 32 and `SchemaContractRatchetTest.noMigrationAboveTheBaselineWritesToATableTheApplicationCannotRead` failed the build: `risk.risk_indicators` (LEGACY), `workflow.workflow_instances` and `workflow.workflow_tasks` (SEED_ONLY) are three of [[F2-141]]'s 36 tables with **no JPA mapping and no Java reference**. That gate's own message is the instruction — *"if the data matters the table needs a mapping first; if it does not, do not ship it"* — and **constraining a table nothing reads protects nothing**. ⚠ The workflow pair is a **near-name trap** and the register is right: the live engine maps `workflow.instances` / `definitions` / `states` / `transitions` / `action_log`, while the dead tables are `workflow.workflow_instances` / `workflow_tasks` — same schema, `workflow_` prefix. **Three generations exist** (`platform.workflow_*` dropped by V114, `workflow.workflow_*` dead, `workflow.*` live), which is [[F2-148]]'s shape. The exclusion is **derived from the committed register**, not hand-listed, so this migration and that gate cannot disagree |
| ⚠ **And this row's own remedy note was wrong — corrected** | It said the 29 non-guard-skipped CHECKs *“need a data audit first”*, reasoning that adding a constraint over violating data fails. True in general, and **irrelevant here**: a database only gains a constraint if it lacks one, and measuring showed **prod holds all 32 and all 53 too** (prod 398 CHECKs / 181 FKs, and 0 of the missing set absent from it). So every `ADD` is a **no-op in both real databases**, and the only database that changes is a fresh install — where the audit that matters is against the chain build, which reports **0 violations across all 32** and every parent table present. 🔑 **I generalised a real hazard without asking which database would be in that state, and made a mechanical change look blocked.** Prod's smaller totals are explained entirely by the 20 migrations pending on it, not by a defect |
| **What V364 does** | 32 idempotent `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT`, **definitions read from dev's own `sys.check_constraints`** rather than composed — a hand-written CHECK that differed from dev's would be a new divergence wearing a fix's clothes. Three self-checks THROW: all 32 present; **none `is_not_trusted`** (so a later `WITH NOCHECK` to get past a violation fails the migration rather than leaving a constraint that covers the next row and not the ones already there); none `is_disabled` (F2-62's dead-flag shape) |
| **Verification** | Applied **twice** to dev (29/29 before and after — a proven no-op) and **twice to the chain-built database (0 → 29, all trusted, all enabled)**. Then enforcement proven in both directions inside a **rolled-back transaction** on the fresh-install database: with `CK_incidents_severity` in place, `severity='BANANA'` is **REFUSED and the error names the constraint**; with it dropped, the same insert is **ACCEPTED** — which is what a fresh install did before V364. After rollback: 0 BANANA rows, constraint present, 0 tagged rows |
| **Provenance** | [[F2-09]]'s table-and-column half reached zero, so the remaining question was constraints. I expected the comparison to be unmeasurable — auto-generated names — and measured the noise floor first: **every CHECK and every FK in both databases is user-named** (0 system-named of 416 and 385), and of the **384 CHECKs present on both sides, 0 differ in definition**. So it is comparable, exactly, and nothing had ever compared it |
| **🔑 The measurement, partitioned against the chain's stop (V320)** | **CHECK: dev 416, built 385.** 32 missing, and **0 of them are explained by the stop** — none is created by a later migration. 29 are named by **no migration anywhere**; 3 are named by V4 and absent anyway. Plus **1 in the other direction**: the migrations create `bcm.bia_assessments.ck_bia_rto_le_mtpd` and **dev does not have it**, so dev can hold a BIA with RTO > MTPD that a fresh install would reject. **FOREIGN KEY: dev 185, built 132.** 53 missing, again **0 explained by the stop**, all 53 named by no migration |
| **🔑 Root cause of the 3, and it is a mechanism not a bug** | `V1__core_schemas.sql:745` creates `cyber.incidents` with `severity NVARCHAR(20) NOT NULL` and no value CHECKs. `V4__incident_module.sql:16` creates it **again**, wrapped in `IF NOT EXISTS (… TABLE_NAME = 'incidents')`, and *that* version carries `CK_incidents_severity`, `_status` and `_category`. On a fresh install V1 wins, V4's guard skips, and **every inline CONSTRAINT in the skipped CREATE goes with it** — so a fresh install accepts `severity = 'BANANA'`. ⚠ **This generalises: any idempotency-guarded re-CREATE of an existing table silently drops its inline constraints.** The guard is working exactly as written; what it also discards is invisible at the call site. Third relative of [[F2-112]] this programme has found — a control that cannot fire |
| **Why the 29 + 53 are absent** | They come from the Python bootstrap (`setup_*_db.py`), which creates tables *with* their constraints, while the migration set's equivalent CREATE omitted them. Same origin as [[F2-140]]'s three tables and [[F2-146]]'s 27 columns: **dev is built by one authority and a customer's schema by another**, and only the objects someone thought to add twice exist in both |
| **⚠ What this finding does NOT claim** | That prod is missing them. Prod descends from a dev dump (baseline 292), so it has dev's constraints — which is precisely why nobody noticed. The population at risk is **a genuinely fresh install**, which is [[F2-143]]'s and [[F2-146]]'s population too |
| **DEFAULT constraints were deliberately not compared** | 1,910 of dev's 2,259 defaults are **system-named** (`DF__table__col__ABC123`), so comparing them by name is noise and comparing by definition would need per-column pairing. Stated rather than silently skipped — the honest scope of this instrument is CHECK and FK |
| **The remedy, in the order that makes it safe** | (1) the 3 guard-skipped CHECKs are a new migration that `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT` them — trivial and safe, dev already satisfies them; (2) the 53 FKs and 29 CHECKs need a **data audit first**: adding a FK to a table that already holds an orphan fails, and this is exactly where a fresh install differs from a populated one, so each needs `WITH NOCHECK` or a cleanup decision; (3) `ck_bia_rto_le_mtpd` is a **product** question — either dev's data violates it or the rule is wrong |
| **Effort** | **M** for (1), **L** for (2)-(3), and (2) cannot be done blind |
| **Verification** | `schema_convergence.py --stop 320` now reports all four buckets per constraint kind. Numbers above are its output. V1/V4 duplication read from source at the line numbers given; V1's version confirmed to carry no CHECK. ⚠ The three `CK_incidents_*` names also appear in **V261's comments only**, and the scan strips comments before attributing — without that, V261 would have been named as their creator |
| **References** | `schema_convergence.py` · `V1__core_schemas.sql:745` · `V4__incident_module.sql:16` · `V261` · [[F2-09]] · [[F2-112]] · [[F2-140]] · [[F2-143]] · [[F2-146]] |
| **Lesson** | **An idempotency guard protects the statement and discards everything the statement carried.** `IF NOT EXISTS … CREATE TABLE` reads as "make sure this table exists"; what it means is "if the table exists, skip its columns, its defaults, its CHECKs and its keys". ⚠ And the methodological half: **I expected this axis to be unmeasurable and checked instead of assuming** — the noise floor was zero, and had I trusted the expectation the whole finding would have stayed invisible. *"Ask of every control: what does it compare, and does that data exist?"* has a companion — **ask of every axis you decline to measure why you think it cannot be measured** |

## F2-152 · A board approval records no approver, and the CFO approval's approver is whatever the request says

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-152 *(measured fixing [[F2-52]]'s last attrition lockout, 2026-08-06)* |
| **Category** | Attribution — [[F2-22b]]'s forgeable-authorship shape, on a three-stage approval chain |
| **Severity** | **P2.** The audit ledger records the acting principal, so the act is traceable; the **record** is not. A quantitative BIA is BCM evidence read by an examiner from the row, not from the ledger |
| **Current State** | ⬜ **Open, filed not fixed.** [[F2-52]] fixed *who may* board-approve; this is *what gets written when they do* |
| **Provenance** | Not sought. F2-52 asked what the board-approve stage records, to judge whether the guard was the only control. It is |
| **🔑 Half one — the board approval has no signer** | `QuantitativeBiaService.boardApprove` sets `status`, `boardApprovedAt`, `boardMinutesRef` and `updatedAt`. **There is no `board_approved_by` column and none is written.** So the row says *a board approved this, at this time, per these minutes* and cannot say who signed. Compare the stage before it, which has `cfo_approved_at`, `cfo_approver_name` **and** `cfo_comments` |
| **⚠ Half two — and the CFO's approver name is supplied by the caller** | `CfoApprovalRequest` carries `@NotBlank String approverName`, written to `cfo_approver_name`. It is never compared to the principal. So the one stage that *does* record a signer records **whatever the request body says** — exactly [[F2-22b]](vi)'s `draftedBy` defect, which the board-pack slice fixed by stamping from the principal and marking the field READ_ONLY. The same fix applies here and was not in this slice's scope |
| **Why the guard is the only control** | `guardTransition` enforces the **order** of the stages (`DRAFT → … → CFO_APPROVED → BOARD_APPROVED`) and nothing enforces that the stages are **different people**. With no approver recorded on the board stage and a forgeable one on the CFO stage, the row cannot even be audited for self-approval after the fact. That is why [[F2-52]] refused `BCM:APPROVE` here: it contains `BCM_MANAGER`, the stage-one role, and the guard was the only thing keeping stage 1 and stage 3 apart |
| **Measured state** | dev `bcm.bia_quantitative`: **1 row, status `CFO_APPROVED`**, `board_approved_at` and `board_minutes_ref` both NULL — the row was parked at the stage the ghost role had closed. So there is **no existing board approval to re-attribute**, which makes the fix additive and cheap |
| **The remedy** | Add `board_approved_by_user_id` (nullable, no default, no backfill — [[F2-109]]/CE-15's position: capacity, never invented attribution), stamp it from the principal, and make `cfoApproverName` READ_ONLY + stamped the way `draftedBy` now is. Then an SoD check across the three stages becomes possible at all |
| **Effort** | **S** for the stamping, **S** for one migration. The reason it is filed rather than done is that adding an approver column while `cfo_approver_name` stays forgeable would leave the chain half-attributed, and both halves belong in one reviewed change |
| **Verification** | `QuantitativeBiaService:221-238` read from source — no approver assignment. `BiaQuantitative` entity: `cfo_approved_at`, `cfo_approver_name`, `cfo_comments`, `board_approved_at`, `board_minutes_ref`, and no board approver field. `CfoApprovalRequest` at `BiaQuantitativeDtos:92`. Live: `EXECUTIVE_REVIEWER` board-approved a cloned row **200 → BOARD_APPROVED** with `minutesRef` and no signer stored |
| **References** | `QuantitativeBiaService#boardApprove` · `BiaQuantitativeController` · `BiaQuantitativeDtos.CfoApprovalRequest` · `BiaQuantitative` · `BiaApprovalChainGuardTest` · [[F2-52]] · [[F2-22b]] · [[F2-109]] · [[F2-151]] |
| **Lesson** | **Fixing who may act is half a control; the other half is what the act records.** Three slices in a row have now found the second half missing right behind the first — [[F2-151]]'s self-declared `attestedRole`, [[F2-150]]'s commander-as-a-label, and here an approval with no approver. **After correcting a guard, read the write path it now admits people to.** |

## F2-151 · No audit-committee member can sign the committee's attestation, and anyone who can may sign as its Chair

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-151 *(measured fixing [[F2-52]]'s audit-committee guards, 2026-08-06)* |
| **Category** | Governance control whose subject cannot operate it, plus an unverified capacity claim |
| **Severity** | **P2.** Latent — `audit_committee.dashboard_snapshot` and `dashboard_attestation` are **0 rows in dev**, so no false attestation exists yet. Structural the first time the committee meets, and the artefact is the one SAMA CG §6 and CMA CG Article 54 require the committee to report from |
| **Current State** | ⬜ **Open, filed not fixed.** [[F2-52]] corrected the guard *names* (see below); the two halves here need a decision this slice deliberately did not take |
| **Provenance** | Not sought. F2-52's slice asked which real role each ghost name meant. `COMPANY_SECRETARY` had a near-miss (`BOARD_SECRETARY`). `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR` and `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER` had none — so the question became *what does the platform know about committee membership?* |
| **🔑 Half one — the Chair and the members cannot attest, and no mechanism admits them** | **No role expresses committee membership.** The roster that could — [[F2-26]]'s `admin.committee_member_terms.member_user_id` — is **NULL on all five audit-committee seats** (committee id 3, `AUDIT_COMMITTEE`), whose `member_name` values are prose: *Mohammed Al-Ghamdi, Nasser Al-Dosari, Sara Al-Qahtani, Head of Internal Audit, External Auditor*. So *“is this user the Chair of the audit committee”* is unanswerable from data, and an entity-bound guard leg would be a control that cannot fire — [[F2-112]]'s shape, which this programme has now met three times ([[F2-112]], [[F2-150]], here) |
| **⚠ Half two — the capacity is self-declared, and it is the more serious half** | `AuditCommitteeDashboardService.attestSnapshot` does `a.setAttestedRole(req.attestedRole())` — **verbatim from the request body**. The signer's *identity* is taken from the principal and hashed (`text \| userId \| ISO-timestamp`), which is right; the **role they signed in is checked against nothing**. `AttestRequest` accepts `CHAIR\|MEMBER\|AUDIT_DIRECTOR\|EXTERNAL_AUDITOR\|COMPANY_SECRETARY` and `CK_ac_att_role` mirrors it. So an admitted `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` — one of the roles the guard *does* let in — can POST `attestedRole: "CHAIR"`, and the platform stores, hashes, audit-logs and F8-publishes an audit-committee **Chair's** attestation. The Chair cannot attest at all |
| **Put together** | The people whose assurance the control exists to capture are locked out, and the people who are let in can claim to be them. That is not a gap in a nice-to-have: an audit-committee attestation is the signature a regulator reads |
| **What [[F2-52]] already fixed, so this row is not overstated** | The write tier was `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR · COMPANY_SECRETARY · PLATFORM_ADMIN` — two ghosts — so generating, resolving and finalising a snapshot was **the platform administrator alone**, while the comment said *“the Chair / Secretary / Platform Admin trio”*. `BOARD_SECRETARY` is now named and the three false comments are corrected. The Chair leg is not restored, on purpose |
| **The remedy, and why it is one decision not two** | Both halves need the same thing: committee membership as data. Either (a) populate `member_user_id` on the roster and gate on *seat*, which also makes `attestedRole` derivable rather than declared — the [[F2-26]] path, and the one that matches SAMA's independence requirements; or (b) seat `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR`/`_MEMBER` as roles, which is cheaper and **wrong in the same way [[F2-145]] refused for `MODEL_OWNER`**: a role says *“some chair”* where the control needs *“the chair of this committee”*. Recommend (a). Also fold in: the capacity vocabulary still says `COMPANY_SECRETARY`, a role name the platform does not have |
| **Effort** | **M** — the linkage API and UI already exist ([[F2-26]]); populating five seats is a tenant-data act, and deriving the capacity is a small service change once the seats resolve |
| **Verification** | `admin.committee_member_terms` for committee 3: **5 seats, 0 with `member_user_id`**. `iam.roles` contains no `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_*` or `BOARD_MEMBER` row in either database. `attestSnapshot` writes `req.attestedRole()` unmodified — read from source at `AuditCommitteeDashboardService:651`. Both tables 0 rows, so nothing to remediate retrospectively |
| **References** | `AuditCommitteeDashboardController` · `AuditCommitteeDashboardService#attestSnapshot` · `AuditCommitteeDashboardDtos.AttestRequest` · `CK_ac_att_role` · `admin.committee_member_terms` · `AuditCommitteeGuardTest` · [[F2-52]] · [[F2-26]] · [[F2-112]] · [[F2-145]] · [[F2-150]] |
| **Lesson** | **A guard that cannot name its subject and a body that lets the caller name themselves are the same defect from two ends.** Both come from the platform not knowing who sits on the committee — and the roster table for it exists, unpopulated. Third time now that asking *“can this be entity-bound instead of role-bound?”* has answered *“there is a column for it and nobody writes it”* ([[F2-112]], [[F2-150]], this). **When a slice cannot bind a guard to an identity, the finding is usually in the data, not the guard** |

## F2-150 · The crisis commander is a free-text label inside a JSON blob, and the column that could name them is empty on every row

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-150 *(measured while fixing [[F2-52]]'s crisis-room guard, 2026-08-06)* |
| **Category** | Identity vs label — the same defect shape as [[F2-26]] and [[F2-113]], one table over |
| **Severity** | **P2.** Nothing is exposed and nothing 500s. The cost is that *“who is commanding this crisis”* cannot be answered by a query, so no guard, notification, escalation or handover can key on it — during the one event where that matters most |
| **Current State** | ⬜ **Open, filed not fixed.** The remedy is a product decision about who a crisis commander is, and a backfill nobody can derive |
| **Provenance** | Not sought. [[F2-52]]'s crisis-room slice asked whether *commander-tier* could be expressed as data rather than as a role list, so I read `bcm.crisis_events`. `crisis_manager_id` exists — and is the answer to that question only if it is populated |
| **🔑 The measurement** | dev `bcm.crisis_events`: **5 rows, `crisis_manager_id` set on 0 of them**. Meanwhile `crisis_team_json` is populated on **5 of 5**, and it names the commander — as prose: `[{"userId":1,"role":"Crisis Manager"},{"userId":2,"role":"Cards Lead"}]`. So the identity is *there* (`userId` is a real id) but the **role is a label**, and the column designed to hold the link is unused |
| **Why the JSON is not good enough** | `"role":"Crisis Manager"` is not `CRISIS_MANAGER`. It is a display string typed by whoever seeded the row, in a JSON array with no CHECK, no FK and no index. Nothing can join it, and a second spelling (`"Crisis Lead"`, `"crisis manager"`) is indistinguishable from a third person. This is exactly what [[F2-113]] had to fix on `committee_referral.recusal_names` — team labels compared against a table of people — and what [[F2-26]] built the roster→user linkage for |
| **What it blocks, concretely** | (a) the crisis-room guard cannot be entity-bound, so it stays a role list — [[F2-52]] recorded that as the reason `BCM:COMMAND` was not invented; (b) `CrisisEventService` cannot notify *the* commander, only a role; (c) a handover between commanders leaves no record; (d) an auditor asking *“who was in command at 02:00”* gets a JSON blob |
| **⚠ What this finding does NOT claim** | That `crisis_manager_id` is dead code — it is a **column with no writer**, which is the [[F2-141]] shape, and the entity may well map it. Nor that the JSON should be deleted: `crisis_team_json` carries the whole team, which no single FK can. The fix is to populate the column **and** give the team array a closed role vocabulary, not to choose between them |
| **Effort** | **M** — the schema change is trivial; deciding whether the commander is a user, a roster seat ([[F2-26]]) or a per-event appointment is not, and the 5 existing rows have no derivable answer |
| **Verification** | `SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(crisis_manager_id) FROM bcm.crisis_events WHERE is_deleted=0` → `5, 0`. `crisis_team_json` non-empty on 5. The five events' team arrays name `userId` 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 with role strings `Crisis Manager`, `Cards Lead`, `CISO`, `Branch Ops Lead`, `Cloud Lead` — three of which are not role names in `iam.roles` either |
| **References** | `bcm.crisis_events` · `CrisisEventController#activeSummary` · `CrisisEventService` · [[F2-52]] · [[F2-26]] · [[F2-113]] · [[F2-141]] |
| **Lesson** | **A role list in a guard and a role label in a JSON blob fail the same way, and finding one is a reason to look for the other.** F2-52 is a programme about names where identities are needed; this is the same defect on the data side of the same feature, and it is why the guard could not be converted to something better than a role list. **When a guard cannot be entity-bound, ask whether the entity actually carries the identity** — twice now the answer has been "there is a column for it and nobody writes it" ([[F2-112]]'s ids that were never written, and this) |

## F2-149 · `external.properties` overrides placeholders, not properties — so the deployment's only config file cannot change most of the configuration

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-149 *(found 2026-08-06 while answering [[F2-92]]'s owner decision; ADR-017 D-16)* |
| **Category** | Configuration mechanism — a control surface that silently does nothing |
| **Severity** | **P2.** It is why a P0's mitigation was inert for four days and the incident record was wrong about the state of a security control. No data exposure; the cost is that operators cannot change what the runbook says they can, and cannot tell |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-06** for the five runtime kill-switches, both config headers, the template and the runbook, with a CI gate. No migration |
| **The defect** | `external.properties` sits beside the jar and is pulled in by `spring.config.import` in `application.yml`. An imported document sits **below** the file that imports it, and a **profile-specific** document (`application-prod.yml`) outranks `application.yml` and everything it imports. So any property path `application-prod.yml` sets **literally** cannot be overridden from the one file operators are told holds all runtime configuration — with no error and no warning |
| **🔑 Why it went unnoticed for months: 18 of the 19 keys work** | Every other key in the deployed file is a `SCREAMING_SNAKE` **placeholder name** that the yml *consumes* — `${DB_URL}`, `${SERVER_PORT:8443}`, `${FLYWAY_BASELINE_VERSION:0}`. A placeholder is a **reference**, resolved against the whole `Environment`, so it picks up a value at any precedence. Those always worked. **The tell was visible in the file: one line in a different style from the other eighteen, and it was the broken one** |
| **⚠ Two config headers asserted the opposite, in prose, and prose is what the operator acted on** | `application.yml` said *"Values defined there win over the packaged defaults … raw spring keys work too"*; `external.properties.template` said *"Any raw Spring key (e.g. `grc.cors.allowed-origins=...`) — full override"*. Both false for a literal profile key. During a P0 an operator wrote `grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=false` on the strength of those sentences; production kept booting with the guard ON and [[F2-92]] recorded the flag as OFF for four days |
| **The blast radius, measured** | `application-prod.yml` has **57 literal scalar settings and 26 placeholders**. **23 of the literals are booleans**, none overridable — and **five are `grc.*` runtime kill-switches**: the tenant write guard and the vuln-SLA, cyber-CAPA-SLA, cyber-evidence-expiry and workflow-request-SLA schedulers. Those five are exactly what an operator needs to stop during an incident, and none of them could be stopped without rebuilding the jar. The other 18 (Swagger off, `flyway.clean-disabled`, secure cookies) are settled policy and **deliberately stay literal** — making them tunable would be a regression, not a fix |
| **The second half: the template documented a third of the surface** | The packaged yml files read **59** `${SCREAMING_SNAKE}` placeholders; the template named **38** (18 active, 20 as commented examples). **21 were absent**, so an operator could not know they existed — including `SWAGGER_ENABLED`, `FLYWAY_DEFAULT_SCHEMA`, `STORAGE_BASE_PATH` and the four `GRC_DB_SIZE_*` thresholds that gate writes as SQL Server Express approaches its 10 GB cap |
| **⚠ A correction to my own first measurement** | I first reported **36** undocumented knobs. That was wrong: my regex matched `^KEY=` and the template documents 20 keys as **commented examples**, which it read as absent. **A scan that treats a comment as absence is the same defect as one that treats a comment as code**, and it inflated the finding by 15 before I re-measured. The honest figure is 21, of which 5 are the switches this fix introduced |
| **What shipped** | The five switches become `${NAME:true}` — **defaults unchanged, all ON**. Both config headers corrected to state the rule. Template gains all 20 missing knobs, each commented with its default and what changing it costs. `DEPLOYMENT.md` §3 carries the rule in a callout. New `ExternalConfigOverrideContractTest`: no template key may name a Spring property path (hard zero), every placeholder the yml reads must be documented (hard zero), the five kill-switches must stay placeholders **and** be documented, and both headers must still state the rule |
| **⚠ Deploying it changes no behaviour** | `application-prod.yml` still defines the path, so the deployed file's stale `grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=false` remains inert, and `TENANT_WRITE_GUARD_ENABLED` is absent so the default `true` applies. The guard stays on, exactly as it is now. Operator action: **delete** the stale line; use `TENANT_WRITE_GUARD_ENABLED=false` if the switch is ever genuinely wanted |
| **Effort** | **S**, and it was already spent |
| **Verification** | Suite **3,368/0/0** · **5 of 5 mutations caught** (raw path added → fails; documented knob removed → fails; guard reverted to a literal → fails; the import mention stripped → fails; the rule wording stripped → fails). ⚠ **The fourth test was broken when written and only the mutation run found it.** Its first version looked for the OLD wording and skipped the check whenever the corrective paragraph was present — which the corrected files always are, so it could fire only if a reverter also deleted the explanation. Rewritten as a **positive** assertion, which cannot go vacuous. And its first green run was against the previous version of the test, so *"4/4 passed"* was true of code I had already replaced |
| **References** | `application.yml` `spring.config.import` · `application-prod.yml` · `external.properties.template` · `ExternalConfigOverrideContractTest` · `TenantWriteGuardConfig` · `DEPLOYMENT.md` §3 · ADR-017 D-16 · [[F2-92]] · [[F2-62]] |
| **Lesson** | **A switch you cannot observe being thrown is not a control.** Nothing in Spring, the log, or the platform reports an outranked property — the operator threw it, the record said OFF, the guard stayed ON, and four days of analysis were spent on the wrong variable. This is [[F2-62]]'s dead flag and A17-D2's fail-open WARN a third time: **a control whose effect is never asserted will eventually be believed rather than known.** And the specific habit worth keeping: when a config file's keys are written in two different styles, the odd one out is the bug |

## F2-93 · The change record says when the CAB decided and never who

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-93 *(found while building A17-D3, because the control D-3 specifies could not be enforced without it)* |
| **Module** | `change_mgmt` |
| **Severity** | **P2** on its own; **blocking** for A17-D3 |
| **Current State** | `change_mgmt.change_requests` carried `cab_decision_at` and `cab_decision_notes` and **no column naming the decider**. The author of a CAB approval, a CAB rejection or an emergency ECAB approval existed only in `platform.audit_log` |
| **Problem** | Two consequences, one obvious and one not. Obvious: an examiner asking *"who authorised this emergency change?"* is answered from a log rather than from the record — and the log is a different retention class from the register. Not obvious: **ADR-017 D-3's segregation-of-duties test had nothing to compare against.** Retrospective ratification exists to supply the independent scrutiny the emergency path skipped; if the emergency approver may also ratify, the control certifies its own author's decision *and* the evidence pack asserts that a second party reviewed it. That is [[F2-29]] one lifecycle step later |
| **Root Cause** | The decision fields were added as *timestamp + free text*. Provenance was treated as an audit concern, and the audit trail genuinely does hold it — which is exactly why nobody noticed the register did not |
| **Fix** | **V345** adds `cab_decision_by_id` / `cab_decision_by_name`, stamped from the authenticated principal on all three CAB-decision transitions — never from a request body (the [[F2-24]] rule). **Not back-filled from the audit ledger**: the ledger holds usernames, not the identity the SoD test compares, and inferring one from the other manufactures provenance for a decision nobody can now attest to. Legacy rows keep NULL, and `GRANDFATHERED` is what stops that NULL being read as "no conflict" |
| **Status** | ✅ **Fixed** — V345, `ChangeManagementService#stampDecisionAuthor`, live-probed (`cabDecisionByName=compliance`, `cabDecisionById=3`) |
| **Lesson** | **A control cannot be enforced against a fact the record does not hold.** The SoD rule was decided in ADR-017 nine days before anyone checked whether the comparison it requires was possible. Measuring the *inputs* a decision needs is part of measuring whether the decision is buildable — the amendment pass checked for ratification columns and missed that the approver was equally absent |


## F2-94 · 126 of 164 automation rules notify nobody — the engine reads `to_role`, the rules all write `roles`

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-94 *(found by A17-D3's live probe: the escalation fired, was audited, and reached no one)* |
| **Module** | `platform/automation` (F8 engine) — affects `change_mgmt`, `policy`, `bcm`, `privacy`, `risk`, `sust`, `socops` and every other module that seeded a rule |
| **Severity** | **P1.** The platform's entire notification/escalation fan-out is inert for 77% of its rules |
| **Current State** | `AutomationActionExecutor.handleNotify` resolves the recipient from `action_json.to_role` (ESCALATE) or `action_json.role` (NOTIFY) — **singular string keys**.
